much pleased with their Surroundings I am very glad to have Jennie So near me it is only a half a mile to her house and we visit each other often Aunt Sallie is still in west Tenn I dont [[inserted: know]] whether She will come back this Spring or not we [[inserted: have]] not heard from her in Some time I [[inserted: have]] been gardening Some but we have had So much Cold weather our vegatables are not doing much good we had quite a Snow Storm yest but the Snow is all gone this morning and it is very pleasant out of doors in the Sun I have Such a lonely time here only a little negro with me Willie is at home of nights but gone every day he is working land over at his Gran Paps this year and is either over there or off with his Waggon hauling for

06-014-P02
Some one [[inserted: all the time]] he never misses a day if he Can help it So you See I am very much confined at home and consequently very lonely. You wished to know the particulars of Cousin Rebeccas Alexanders death I did not know She was Sick until the night before She died I was at the funeral and learned there that She exposed herself getting up very early of mornings to look at the Comet which She was very much interested about She took a very Severe Cold and died from the effect of it I think She was in her right mind all the time during her Sickness Sat up eat her breakfast and talked with her friends in the morning and died that evening a few a Clock, As to the Lawsuit I know very little about it only you know just what I hear [[inserted: hearsay]] other People Say

06-017 | manuscript
Source: ACU CRS MS5 - 06 - Folder 3, Correspondence and Legal Papers.pdf | PDF scan page 17
06-017-P01
Readyville Tenn March the 3 1878
Miss Lizzie Douglas
My very dear Cousin
Your kind and interesting letter came to hand in due time and I hasten to reply. This leaves the family in rather poor health, Pap & Mother are both Complaining and the Children all have the Whooping Cough. Willie has it very bad and besides that he has had a spell of billious fever is sitting up a little this morning for the first time in Several days. Adele is quite sick with the Cough She has it the second time. Cousin Nellie is getting better but Charles Children are very bad off. Well the wedding Came off at the appointed time we had nice Crowd a good supper and every thing passed off quietly. Adele Willie and myself all went to the reception At Cousin Miriams they had a splendid dinner and all seemed to enjoy it very much Jimmie & Mary are going to live with Cousin Miriam as She is almost alone having only one Child single and he is hardly ever at home Jimmie and Mary Came over yes evening they are both well they have [[inserted: gone]] to Church to day at newhope We had Some fun out of them this morning

06-017-P02
[[margin]]
you must excuse all errors as the Children have kept up such a noise and talking I could hardly write at all will try to do better next time
Yours as ever
L A J
[[/margin]]

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continues on scan 18. The postscript is inverted above the opening date.

on different days so we can go every Sunday if we like Mr Barr and Aunt Jane Came up and Spent a night with us last week they were both very well and their Children were all well Aunt Jane is very much broken and look old and feeble Mr Barr looks pretty much the same has for the last five years. Marybee went to Readyville last week and [[deleted: illegible]] her picture taken to send to [[obscured: smudge]] you She was going to write to you this evening but some of her beaux coming in She will have to defer writing untill an other time Well Cousin I was very much surprised when I saw the Money you sent me I never dreamed of such a thing as your Ma selling the saddle but as you say money never comes amiss I was very glad to get it. Charlie and family are all getting on finely Little Alma is a sweet little thing and talks quite plain She favors her gran ma very much Charlie is Still my Bro and friend I would go see him often poor fellow but I have less use for his lady than any woman I ever saw though I try to be friendly with her for his sake but I have said to much already and will Stop you must write soon and tell me all the news give my love to all the kin tell them if I live I am coming to see them I must bring the Children all send much love to you I will close as it is late
Ever your friend and cousin
L A Jetton

Saturday 19th Lizzie I expected to write a good deal sooner than I have but since I stoped the other night circumstances have been such that it would be inconvenient to do Grand ma was taken very sick night before last and was quite sick yesterday though is up this morning Bud John had a chill night before last but I hope as the weather is getting cool we will not be troubled much with chills.
I didn't know until a little while ago that one of the family would be going to town to day so I will have to close hurriedly—I expect to have company this winter Aunt Jane and her family (Jennys own mother) expect to move out in a few weeks. her husband and two of her daughters and their families have gone to California Uncle J. has only gone to look at the country if he likes it he will move Aunt J. and the children out They are coming to stay here until he returns or sends for them. So will have two young lady Cousins with us and little one enough to keep music all the time I reckon it will be right hard for us to get used to the noise of Children we have been living so quiet the boys in the field the most of the time leaving Grandma and me alone. I'm very anxious to go to school this winter but will not be able to do so I want Pa to send the little boys if possible for they are getting to be big boys

My dear Lizzie
After so long, long a silence I will [[obscured: ink blot]] now endeavor to converse a little with you through the medium of my pen. What is the cause of this silence? Am I to blame? if I am I am sorry for it But did I not answer your last letter? My Dear Lizzie

[[illegible]] much more lively but it has been sickly last week we were all able to be up at one time but we couldn't hold out at that some body had to be sick so Frank and I both took chills I did not but one but have been feeling badly every other day Frank still continues to have them had one last night and has high fever now he has a hard time of it has been sick a great deal this summer I am afraid it will get us in to hard spells of fever Bud Davy has a chill

Your very welcome letter of the 25th July reached me about two weeks ago I read it while in bed I have been quite sick was in bed nearly a [[illegible]] it [[illegible]] caused from billiousness being sick when I got your letter and very busy since I got well I hope you will excuse me for not answering it sooner I have only partially regained my strength I am greatly reduced in flesh and very much reduced in color My sickness has served to make me look like an Ala. girl the first morning that I was able to fill my seat at the table some of them said “Cousin Lizzie your sickness shows right smartly on you” I said “Oh! it is only helping to make an Ala. girl of me” it seemed like they were going to [[inserted: quiz]] me they all commenced “yes you never have any sickness in Texas” said I “we dont have as many pale faces there as you do here” I was sick two weeks last summer but it didn't take

06-050-P02
[[separate block: left-hand page; concluding page of this letter]]
it out I would have liked so much to have gone I dont know whether there is an organized church and regular preaching down there or not if there is I hope we will get to go yet I havnt met up with any one yet who is a member of the Christian Church Pa and I are alone it makes me feel right badly I do wish there were a church in this neighborhood or even if it were not in this neighborhood if it were near enough for us to attend once in a while that would be better than not to go at all we have very good Methodist preaching here as there are none but Methodists living here we dont have series of doctrinal sermons like they do at Liberty
Lizzie do you ever hear anything from Mr. Goodman these days poor man I reckon he will move and move until he settle in his grave and leave his family helpless it is a pity that he cant be contented to stay in one place I feel sorry for him and family Where is Mr. Austin and what is he doing any thing? he is very much related to Mr. goodman Lizzie I have written a letter to Jane and Mary which I hope you will pardon me for sending in yours give it to any of or all the boys and they will get some person to read it for them you can read it if you want to before you give it to them I hardly knew how to begin or how to end please write me a long letter I have written two [[illegible]] this contains more to write with much love yours Lizzie

Dear Lizzie
I expect some of the family will go to town tomorrow and I will try and scratch you a few lines I would have written before now but I received Mollie's letter about two weeks ago she said you had received my letter I have been looking for the reply I had much rather answer a letter than to write before receiving one I heard last week that there were letters in the office for me but when we sent for them [[deleted: illegible]] we couldn't get any So I supposed one of them was from you so I will try and write you something if only enough to bring you in debt to me you will therefore excuse this uninteresting letter for I know I shall fail to interest you as there is no news afloat and but little family news none of the Cousins married yet and not probable that any of them will be soon we are all well at this time except Pa he has had sore eyes very bad but they are improving now I very much feared he would entirely lose one of them at least but now they are so much better I hope he will save both of them When I wrote to Mollie last I was not quite well had two or three chills but broke them up with red pepper

My dear Lizzie
I commence a letter to you tonight, not knowing when I will finish it. I have made several attempts to reply to your letter of the 11th Oct. but there has always been something to prevent my carrying out my design I have been very busy, and then, we have such a large family, that we never have a quiet moment until bed time. and then I do not feel like writing [[deleted: illegible]]
I reckon you have heard of the additions to Grandma's household—my Aunt & family at first [[deleted: the]] noise of so many children annoyed me, but now I am used to it I reckon I will hardly know what to do with myself when they go away. have any doubt but what they will take ours. It is now currently reported and believed, that the wheat which the Farmers carried in before the tythe tax, was due, in order that the Soldiers might get some flour has been sold by speculators. They say they would manage it this way; they would [[store?]] it [[illegible]] where a board would be appointed to examine it. They would condemn it as inferior flour, and it would be sold, they would then sell it at an enormous price and pocket the proceeds. There was a man here the other day from Nacochitoches who says this is so, and that Magruder is at the head of it. 06-069 | manuscript
Source: ACU CRS MS5 - 06 - Folder 3, Correspondence and Legal Papers.pdf | PDF scan page 69
06-069-P01
Brushy April 21st 1865
Dear George:

06-069-P02
We were somewhat surprised last tuesday evening — the 18th by the arrival of Joda; we were all truly glad to see him you may be sure. I was a little disappointed in not getting a letter from you, but suppose you have written by mail since your return from Velasco. I am anxious to hear something about Dock, and the something you would tell of next time which you spoke of in yours of the 5th inst. has accomplished its purpose — excited my curiosity. The thread you sent by J. M. was very acceptable, it will save me many a turn of my “Piano.” The pins — although I had plenty you left before — do not come amiss. I have a little speculation in my head, which, if I was sure it would turn out right, I would write you several little articles to buy that you might keep your eyes open for such bargains: but, as I am not sure of accomplishing it, I will just tell you my plan. It is to send down some flour by Joda that Laura and I have. There is only six hundred pounds of it, and Joda says if he gets Transportation at all, he will take it. But he does not know yet whether he will get any thing to transport, untill he hears from Mr Bell. If he takes a waggon we will try to send you a little something to sweeten your tooth. I would like for you to look around a little, and see if a side saddle could be got in Houston. Laura is very anxious to get one, and if the flour speculation succeeds she might stand a chance to get one, as Joda says waggons are continually passing from Houston to Dallas

====================================================================
06-070 | manuscript
Source: ACU CRS MS5 - 06 - Folder 3, Correspondence and Legal Papers.pdf | PDF scan page 70
06-070-P01
I recd a letter from Laura this evening. she seems to be very well satisfied in her new situation. says she has from 16 to 19 schollars, with a prospect for more. I suppose it is better than to be carding and spinning but take me from friends and Home, and place me among strangers, and I would feel that I was left to pine neglected, and to “perish in forgetfulness” — to be poetical. Cousin Mollie has just returned from school and is going to stay all night with me so I must quit.

06-070-P02
Saturday evening 22nd Today has been bright and clear, quite an uncommon thing: the wind has been from the north since day before Yesterday, and last night we had frost enough to kill most of our beans, though I do not think the fruit is injured. Cousin M. amused me last night by relating some of her school exploits, and altogether the time was passed off quite pleasantly. She is going to Liberty; A mrs. Bishop is teaching there now. She is from Dallas, and some rather quiter, I mean — could teach almost every thing the Dead Languages included. But May says it is with difficulty she can find the answers in old Kirkham, so I suppose the Living have become Dead to her. Some foul play has been carried on, up here of late. Several horses have been stolen, and two Stiles boys who lived over in the neck and were deserters, were suspected. A company of men got after them, and caught one of them — the Youngest; he acknowledged to stealing and said his brother was concerned in it. They hung him on the same limb Stanley was hung on — so we have heard. They tell various tales about the other. one is that they shot him and broke his arm but did not take him. Another, that they took him, and hated to shoot him while a prisoner, so they guarded him loosely so he would try to make his escape, which he did. and then they shot him and broke his arm but he made his escape

EDITORIAL NOTE: The account of violence explicitly includes hearsay (“so we have heard”) and alternative stories. These are the writer’s reports; no independent verification is implied. Text continues on scan page 71.

06-071 | manuscript
Source: ACU CRS MS5 - 06 - Folder 3, Correspondence and Legal Papers.pdf | PDF scan page 71
06-071-P01
Last Sunday morning a party of 8 or 10 men passed Mrs Campbells — aunt [[Bats?]] house — with one of the Stileses. Jim Floyd was one of the party. a young man who was at Mrs Campbells asked Floyd what they were going to do with him. He replied, they were going to take the left hand road with him. The same day Jennie Bell saw a party enter the big thicket at their wood yard. They either took him in there and hung him, or went in to hunt him, after he made his escape. One thing is very certain to my mind, that is if they ever captured him, he never made his escape. Perhaps they merited death, but I dread the consequences of this mob law. We know not, but this is the beginning of terrible times. I hate the thought that Brushy [[deleted: should]] should be the place of the beginning of such things. I would feel a great deal better if I knew that man was not hanging over in that thicket.

06-071-P02
Fayette has not yet returned; the last news from them, Bob was having the chills, and was trying to get a furlough to come with F.

06-087-P01
[[Wednesday?]] night 15th This beautiful day has been passed very busily and pleasantly by me, we have been putting in a piece of cloth, and this evening [[Colburn?]] and Henry R. came over. [[Colburn?]] came to stay all night to go a turkey hunting with Joda in the morning, but was disappointed as Joda went to Dallas to day to see Watts having failed to see him at Ingeville as he went to Johnson; but they have let their plans to have a good hunt while Joda stays. You ought to be here to hear the turkeys gobble of a morning and see some of our beautiful pet deer. They are very gentle, since you have ceased to torment them. We also have another pet up in these western thickets, which [[illegible]] we suppose to be a panther. There are a kind of pets I would rather would be a little more distant. On the subject of John Turneys, the people of [[Tennessee?]] are anxious that he shall get a six mule team if he can, if not two four mule teams; They seem anxious to send plenty up there to the Co.

06-087-P02
Yours of March 30th we recd last Sunday. You say dont get too fast on the peace questions I will not, for I never was as sanguine as Father and [[Louisa?]] we all told them they were too fast. But I always have and always will think there is something wrong about this cotton trade. You have seen before this the account of the threatened invasion of Tex. from Ark. of twelve thousand men with a train of four hundred waggons. I rather reckon you have not seen the accounts of the wise disposal Genl McCullough has made of his men of late; or such items as these seldom go through the Telegraph. He appointed a day for them all to rendezvous at a certain place. Some of them being at home on furlough two hundred of them had arrived when they were surrounded by a Regmt and taken prisoners and then sent off to their respective commands where they had originally belonged, or to their enrolling officers. just turned out as I always expected it. un-fortunately a great many had not got there when the two hundred were captured. [[deleted: among them William Duff and his]] nephews Jno Smith who have returned to this section and report the [[illegible]]. They have joined Co. with [[illegible]]. This movement on the part of McCullough has rendered these men desperate. Rome has now gone to Wax. with a waggon master who he is acquainted with and who he thinks is his best friend, to try to get to drive a team from San Antonio to Eagle Pass. they say the Govt wants men who will bring their own teams. It will suit with R. if he can get into it but I cant help but think it is a trick to get him into the Service, though it may turn out that my fears are all groundless.

06-089 | manuscript

06-089-P01
Brushy Nov. 13th 1864
Dear George

06-089-P02
You will have to forgive my delay, my excuse is busy times. This morning Lou and I went to meeting to Liberty to hear Mrs Justins funeral preached; it was to have been preached at the Colony last Sunday, but Mr Haynes had been sick and was not able to preach. To day the house was cramed jamed and running over. A goodmany of the Colony were up and a greatmany from about Shilo. Five preachers: Haynes, Justin, Maley, White, and Berry. Mr Haynes gave us a long tedious discourse from the last clause of the 4th vs. of the 11th ch. Hebrews. He spoke fully two hours, and a good portion of his sermon was about the depreciation of the currency (I am not talking about the “old” and “new issue”) but the money itself. The “old issue” was fully represented to day; and judging from the display have no idea of being repudiated soon. Em. and Liz. were there I just got to speak to them, had no time to talk. I wish you had been there to see all of the people. Times are about as they were when you were here; a good deal of work to do and not much time to visit. We assisted aunt Bettie in getting ready to move, she did not get her thread ready for me to weave, but got some jeans from Ellen, and we made the little boys coats. She got off on the morning of the 10th

06-090 | manuscript
Source: ACU CRS MS5 - 06 - Folder 3, Correspondence and Legal Papers.pdf | PDF scan page 90
06-090-P01
She took Betsy and chickens, left the spinnack and what few cows she had. I think [[her will intend?]] coming back to attend to them. Father bought a sow and five shoats from her for ten dollars specie, so I reckon we are safe in the meat line for another year. — that is if we can get corn raised to feed them on. Father has reserved twenty acres for [[corn?]] and hungarian. Laura wrote to you, Gibson was to fix the fence; she was mistaken that was not in the bargain; he was just to raise the wheat, cut it and thrash it and put a fourth in the granary. How the old fence is ever to be fixed up is more than I can tell but I hope it will all come out right. The well holds out finely about a dozen mules and horses are watered out of it twice and three times a day. It gets down pretty low, but hardly gets muddy, and by the next time is as full as ever. If I had any hopes of the war ending soon I would feel so much better but from the tone of the papers, we need not look for peace in four more years. Old Abe is elected in all probability and [[Childsy?]] thinks it is best for if Mc. Clelland is elected says he, propositions will be made which some of the States will accept, and then we are ruined. So it seems he is for four more years warfare.

06-090-P02
The wind was blowing cold from the north on last monday evening we were all sitting round the fire, when we heard [[coo a night owl?]] we looked out and sure enough there she was. [[Childsy?]] was nearly frozen, but a warm fire soon set him to talking, and he and Mr Grounds (a soldier that came with him) kept us laughing nearly all the time they were here.

My paper is full and I will have to quit I reckon you are wishing I had. I cant send this to the office before Sunday. Affectionately Lizzie

06-094-P01
Brushy Texas No. 4
Feb. 19th 1864.
Brother George:

06-094-P02
Yours of the 7th and 8th came to hand this evening, and although short, gave us great satisfaction. When the Sundays mail fails to bring us any letters, as it did last Sunday, we are always uneasy until we do hear from you. Brushy has been in the receipt of various news to day; Laura got a letter from Fayette, M Orr one from Fayette, Mary and I one apiece from Jim.

06-094-P03
They have come safely through all the fights except the slight wound Jim rec. at Chickamauga. They both say they are tired of it. Jim says “he can stand the fatigue and hardships all very well, till it comes to the fighting fighting, and then when he sees his comrades falling around him, it is all he can do to persuade himself not to run.” Tole Hamilton fell at Ringold, in the retreat. he was shot through the breast, and only lived a few minutes. Poor fellow he has gone like many another from home and kindred, never more to return. He leaves a widow and child. The boys write home that two Goodloes (Aquilla’s sons) have deserted. And whose name do you expect to hear [[illegible]]? Tell no other than Squire. but uncle [[Givans?]] says this must [[illegible]] out of the family I know not why unless his boys wrote it home is the reason. But Squire is safe over the Border, where a many another poor Dixie boy wishes he was I expect. But Squire is not the only one of your acquaintance. The boys say that Charly Brown has written to them, that Will is safe with his kindred in a Northern Clime, hearty and well. Now dont you reckon that Will G. and Will Brown are having a happy time? Mary G. is perfectly satisfied about Billy. From the tone of Jodas letter, he seems to think your Batt. is disgraced worse than any other body of men in the Army, but he is behind the times, and had as well quit his noise. Tom [[Warthen?]] writes home that they have to keep a guard round Gurleys reg. to keep them from deserting. We hear there all of Murrays Texas Co. have left but Sixteen. 06-097-P01
No. 13.
Brushy, June 28th 1864.
Dear Brother,

06-097-P02
I have sorrowful news to tell you this morning. Uncle Alfred is dead. Mr Orr recd a letter from Henry yesterday, confirming what we had heard before. He died late Sunday evening the 5th of this month, just 18 days after he was wounded. Poor Aunt Bettie is allmost crushed beneath the blow. As soon as she heard it was really true, she fainted away, and they thought for a while she would never revive again. Ever since, she has had cramping spells, and sometimes loses her breath. I have just returned from there, Mary Orr and I staid with her last night. I fear she will have a severe spell of sickness first — if she ever does get over it.

06-097-P03
He writes that the Drs made a good examination of his wound just a few days before he died, (which they had not been permitted to do previously, on account of the swelling) and discovered that the bone had been considerably fractured, just below the knee cap, and upon pressing it a good deal of matter run out with the oil of the knee cap.

Sue

Nancy Hancock, (Stout that was) was taken sick on Sunday and died on the next wednesday. They say after she died her eyes poped out of her head. While they were going to bury her, her little brother was taken suddenly, and died [[deleted: illegible]] in two hours he had had a chill or two before, but got up and helped to catch a chicken that morning and ate a hearty breakfast. It is a strange disease. They did not complain of any pain.

06-110-P01
Mr. Telly — Nancy [[Culphers?]] husband — has been in bad health for a long time: on last Sunday morning a small red spot made its appearance on his arm, it spread rapidly and his arm swelled all over, mortification took place and he died on monday. I have heard of other sudden deaths, it is all thought to be the same disease, in different forms. J. Bell is now suffering severely from his wound. His shoulder is greatly swelled, and there is a place six inches long, in which he says he can feel the ball working back and forth. They think the ball will have to be cut out, but the Dr. thinks he had better not do it till the weather gets cooler.

06-110-P02

He came riding up through the rain, which had been falling nearly all morning; he was in such a hurry he did not stay more than fifteen minutes, we wanted him to stay for dinner but he was in such a hurry he did not want to [[deleted: illegible]] talk about it. I reckon thats the way they all are when they get pretty close home. He will get home to night, says he left Sabine on the 31st thats only seven days on the road. Dont you call that pretty good traveling.

Thirty days is a short time for a man to come so far, he would not have long to stay at home but a short time is better than none. I am glad old Magruder is gone.

06-111 | manuscript
Source: ACU CRS MS5 - 06 - Folder 3, Correspondence and Legal Papers.pdf | PDF scan page 111
06-111-P01
I will now have to tell you something more about the meetings which seem to be the most engrossing events of the day up this way. Every one preaches his own doctrine with all his might, consequently discussion [[inserted: is]] [[deleted: illegible]] rife. You wondered in one of yours, whether the good feeling which seemed to exist between different parties would continue to exist. I will give you a few items and you can draw your own conclusions: At our meeting in August it was announced that at the next appointment the meeting would be protracted, several eminent preachers were expected, and of course good preaching anticipated. Now this was not exactly in accordance with the feelings of our Methodist friends, so after studying on it awhile they appointed a meeting in Mr. [[Batakers?]] neighborhood embracing the same time! Not exactly as warm towards us as of yore, think you? The saying of Parson Hill, “now if me and my neighbor dont agree I just let him alone, dont go about him,” had sunk deep in their hearts, so union meetings were forgotten. Our meeting commenced at the appointed time, thursday night before the 1st Sunday. the congregations were small untill Sunday when, notwithstanding their efforts at “hedging” there were so many there, they had to move the seats out and preach under the grove. It is only the methodists that are so hostile. the presbyterians are not so afraid of the truth.

06-111-P02
Bro Jones was [[inserted: the]] only preacher from a distance, he did most of the preaching. By request Parson Austin addressed the people Sunday evening, [[inserted: he preached]] from the words “It is finished”. He made a very good talk. There were no conversions, but four united with the church — Milton Rawlins, his wife, Sarah Selby, and Lizzie [[Burnard?]]. The meeting closed on monday night at which time Bro Jones preached one of the best sermons I ever heard on the unity of the church. The house was full and I hope a good

07-003 | letter
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 3
07-003-P01
No 10
Brushy Wednesday Night
April 15th /63
Dear Brother:
Again I take my pen to write, though I will not promise to be very interesting. Laura received your letter of 21st March last Saturday, the first letter we had got for three weeks. Lou got Joda’s letter last Sunday with yours of the 12th inst. enclosed which gave us great satisfaction; as we did not know whether you had left Galveston or not. I hope your new situation will prove a healthy, and agreeable one, though, fear it will not be so much so as the one you left. Do you think there is any probability of your being attacked there, in that inland place? it looks to me [[deleted: to a curious place for]] soldiers. I fear you will not remain there long, but be ordered along untill you get to the Mississippi and there be trapped up like the Post prisoners were or perhaps receive a worse fate.

07-003-P02
You cannot imagine how uneasy we were when we could not hear from you; how many causes were assigned for not getting letters. Who knew but what some of your letters had been read, or some of

07-004 | letter continuation
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 4
07-004-P01
mine to you, and something dreadful been done to you; for you may have been careless with them, leave them lying about, and who knows how much treason might be found in some of our uncongenial ideas. So reasoned Mother and what truthfulness there was in her logic time alone could determine. I know you will smile when you read this, but you must remember how scary we allways are when any thing unusual happens. Moreover, Mother has enjoined upon me, to be careful what I put on paper, in these perilous times: and, by the by just while I think of it, Beck told us she found several of my old letters in Warrens trunk. had, nt you better, after you have perused them to your hearts content, just commit them to the flames of your camp fire; they will only raise the blaze a little higher and then settle down and be out of mischief.

07-004-P02
After hoeing so hard all day, and then brought a buckett of water from the head spring and then milked the cows (we have six young calves in the pen) I feel right smartly fatigued so for the present, hopeing you are not on guard to night, I make my best bow and retire.

07-004-P03
16th This is a very pretty evening, the clouds that obscured the Sun for a while this morning, have been driven away by a strong southern breeze.

and left the sky clear and bright. We have had a very seasonable spring so far, consequently every thing looks well. Fathers six acres of corn happened to be planted just before a big rain; it has come up beautifully, scarcely a missing hill. Mr. Graves did not do quite so well, he had to replant a good deal.

07-005-P02
Cousin Gran got home on the 4th inst. on a sixty days furlough; it appears to me, Gran must be born to good luck; this is the second time he has been home for sixty days since they all went to Arkansas. I mean being married goes a long ways in his favor in getting furloughs it appears. There is Lambert Pace, has been sick for a long time, and has been trying to get to come home, but had not got permission at last accounts, just because he is not married I suppose. Joda writes he expects to [[lost: small tear]] to come home about the middle of May; You say nothing at all about coming, so I suppose there is no chance for you to come.

07-008 | letter
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 8
07-008-P01
Saturday Night April 4
Dear George:
Warrens stay is about over with us, as he starts tomorrow; and I thought I would write you a few lines to let you know we are all stirring. We have not received a line from you for about two weeks, I cant tell why it is we dont get letters unless they have stopped you from writing; yet I hope this is not the case. We were filled with sadness this evening by hearing of the death of Mrs Payne. Poor woman to die and leave her little children to meet the worlds cold frowns without a mothers kind and tender care there is five of them one an infant of one week old. Preston is at home now though as a matter of course he will have to go back to the army soon

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continues on 07-009. Year not written; the later slip suggests 1863.

07-009 | letter continuation
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 9
07-009-P01
We send you two pairs of socks and some pills and a fine [[deleted: comb?]] comb. I wish we could send something else but I have been studying and can think of nothing else that would be of any benefit to you; as you seemed to like the cotton socks Ellen gave you we thought we would knit some more thinking they would be more pleasant for summer. If you do not like them I suppose you have woollen socks enough to do you till we can send you more. Sister is over and Warren being here it only lacks your presence and Jodas to make us seem as we used to seem. Oh! I do hope the time will come when you can again be with us; but if you have gone east I fear it will be a long time first. As I wrote you a long letter by last yesterdays mail I can write no news of interest to nite.
Your Sister Lizzie

Brushy Tex.

Dear Brother.
Again I take my pen to write you a few lines, though I dont promise to be very interesting. I have written you four letters, and never have received a line from you yet. We have been looking anxiously for letters for the last week and none have come. Laura went to the Post Office this evening and I thought sure we would get a letter but as usual we were disappointed. 07-014 | later typescript of letter
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 14
07-014-P01
Letter Number 9/ Tuesday night Feb. 10, 1863
Dear George,
I recieved your letter of Feb. 1 this evening, letter, map, and all very interesting. Ellen was delighted with her letter. She has had us read it for her at least ten times this evening, you must write her another, it does her so much good as it does me to get a letter. I recieved your letter of 25 Jan. a week ago to day, and by a continuation of dates will try to answer them both in the same letter.

07-014-P02
I believe we have never written to you about hearing from Aunt Rebecca Hymann’s folks. As Jessie was returning from Ark. he camped with a man just from Miss. who told him, the Federals had overrun aunt Rebecca’s neighborhood destroyed her farm, and had taken her house for a hospital; her boys were all in the army or had been. Henry was at home on account of his having been wounded at Ft. Donaldson(?)

07-014-P03
Mollie O. Sue, Laurer, and myself all went over to hear parson Austin last Sunday. He gave his views on the Millenium made a pretty good talk I suppose; but I didn’t understand much of it; came home and heard Mr orr had recieved a letter from Henry so we ate a few bites and went down to see what he had written: his letter was dated 21 and 23 Jan. they were at Pine Bluff had been there only a few days, they left the White River country in a hurry, he said their cooking utensils were strown from Brownsville to Little Rock their teams having given out so they could not pull them. We have not heard Fayett’s and Jim’s fate. Henry wrote he had talked with several who had made their escape, who told

The question mark after Ft. Donaldson is in the typescript. 07-015 | later typescript of letter
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 15
07-015-P01
him they had seen Fayett and Jim late in the evening on the first day of the fight in the rifle pits, all right then; that is the last account we had of them.

07-015-P02
Wednesday night, 11 Henry allso wrote that cousin Granville had seen Jack Chappell he had made his escape from Ark. Post he said he was detailed to dig ditches, and when he saw the Federal flag waving over town he got out; he was on his way to Little Rock and was going to try to get from there home. Burdet Weatherford and John Porter have got home, they say they were detailed to wait on the Dr. at the hospital and as soon as they saw the Federal flag flying they allso left. Porter says he lay in the bushes near there for a day and a night perhaps, and that after the Feds. got possession, the men in the rifle pits kept firing at them, so one of the gunboats moved a little further down the river, and just raked the ditches and our officers had to call out, Stop men stop! before the rifle men would desist. Aunt Cynthia is very uneasy about Jim and Fayette. We have been spooling our thread today for our dresses tomorrow we expect to mark it, and as Mr Tilford is to bring our loom home tomorrow we expect to get out cloth in next day. it is now eight o’clock so I must quit as they have all gone to bed but me.

07-015-P03
Saturday 14 Feb.
Your letter of the sixth just came to hand this morning: glad to hear you are enjoying good health. Well, I find I must try to lengthen my epistles, draw them out, spin a longer thread in other words, try to compose a little. Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 16
07-016-P01
I will try to be more interesting.

07-016-P02
You ask “what I think of such opinions” as are advanced by your leader, I answer to say the least, They are arbitrary, unjust and tyrannical. Let such minds as these go into ascendency and have controll and where is our liberty, our privilege as rational beings? I answer gone! and gone forever!
I am sorry you are under command of one, who has so little feeling, so little humanity, and has so much tyranny of opinion about him; if he really thinks what he says, if he does not, I detest his moral principal as a man, and think him unfit for the position which he occupies. If he was to see this, I suppose he would be more of the opinion than ever, THAT correspondence should be stopped between the “utencils” of war and their equally worthless friends at home; for my part about all the good I wish him is, that he may never rise to higher command but sink to the position of one of the lowest high privates and then let him tyrannize over whom he can.

07-016-P03
As for peace, it is what we cannot hope for, as long as the North choose to prosecute their present undertaking and the South holds out with it’s stubborn resistance. Oh! that the ruling powers would stop! Stop and think for what this strife is for! for what this stream of blood continues to flow. But no, of this they do not think: the love of power is stronger than any other, and all must Subserve to this. We cannot stop it, we can only move along with this vast current and trust to providence to bring us safely through. May the time speedily come when peace shall again smile upon us is my prayer.

07-016-P04
Saturday night, my usual time for writing to you, has again arrived. Sue, Laura, and myself all writing, Mother is knitting. Father and the Children in bed.

That regiment appears to be composed of not very sound matierial any how from all I can learn, it is doubtful whether the Confederacy is ever benefitted much by thir service.

Saturday 14th Feb.
Your letter of the 6th inst. came to hand this morning: glad to hear you were enjoying good health. Well, I find I must try to lengthen my epistles, draw them out spin a longer thread; in other words, try to compose a little. As for my ever becoming a newspaper correspondent, it is something to which I will never hope to attain: my brain is not full enough of ideas to try to communicate them to the masses, even if I had language at my controll by which to do so: but can't is a word, which should be in no ones vocabulary, therefore in the future, I will try to be more interesting.

This is a beautiful day the wind is from the north quite cool for this time of year the sun is shining very brightly every thing looks so green and pretty, though I suppose I need not expatiate on the beauties of nature, as you are now in sight of trees and vegetation, and not surrounded by a waste like you were on the Island. This good weather is very appreciated, we have had such a wet spring and the wheat had a little rust: I wish you could see Jims wheat it looks so fine. Some of it comes up to Jeffies chin, the birds are eating it some now. Harvest will soon be here, some talk of cutting this week (the Becketts and Lemmons) but ours will not be ready before two or three weeks yet: I hardly know how people will get their grain saved unless the men are furloughed there surely are not enough of men here to save all of the grain.
I have just been out to get Laura some dewberries. They are very scarce as the prairies are nearly all plowed up. Our garden looks very well plenty of mustard lettuce and radishes now and we will have plenty of beans peas squashes and tomatoes we planted a good many onions but they are not doing well

07-033 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 33
07-033-P01
Mr Orr got a letter from Mr Dyer the other day. He writes that John says cousin Robert Jetton died in Miss. three of Uncle Louis's boys, he says, were taken prisoners at Ft. Donaldson but had been exchanged and were back in Tennessee when he left there. John Jetton from inability, had never been in the army. I think John Orr must be mistaken about three of uncle Louis's boys being taken prisoners, for I do not think there were but two at Ft. Donaldson. But all is now hid behind the “vail of futurity”; when that is raised the picture may be sickening to look upon: how many may then be dead whom we have known since childhood, time alone can tell. O that this awful war would cease, and let those who are yet alive return to their homes.
It appears to me, there has lives enough been sacrificed to gratify the ambition of any man that has any heart at all but I suppose Lincoln does not care if the lives of every man in the South are sacrificed if he gets his beloved colored [[deleted: citizens]] liberated, and he can rule this Southern land. It is for who shall rule and who shall not they are fighting for, and not for the love of the union; but I think I would be willing to live under the rule of the Czar of Russia to get peace. Most any thing would satisfy me, but the setting of the negroes free here among us, that would be more than human nature could stand: if (old Lincoln) intends to make us and the negroes equals I want the South to fight him till he gets out of the notion, and then take him and make him serve in the capacity of one the ballance of his days. It seems all hopes of foreign intervention has failed entirely; and it remains now to fight fight till one side gives it up, or the other is conquered. I hope it will not be the latter for I do not think a conquered people could be happy: just think of a standing army over us to keep down insurrection. Should we gain our independence would it be desirable or not, I mean would the independence gained be desirable, there would be a standing army to support, a conscription term to serve if our president could carry out the views advanced before the Miss. Legislature.

07-033-P02
[[separate block: inverted upper margin]]
I got a letter from aunt Jane the other day. She and the children were well she said she had got a letter from you a short time before

07-036 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 36
07-036-P01
Letter No. 9.
Brushy Texas April 2nd 1863.
Dear Brother:
It has now been near two weeks since we received a letter from you; and you may imagine how anxious we are to hear from you, your whereabouts & C. as your last letter stated you would leave Galveston in a few days.
I cannot tell, why it is, we have not got letters lately unless it is the fault of the mails, as there has been a great deal of high water lately. Last Saturday and Saturday night it rained very hard harder at some places than it did the other big rain on the 25th Feb. but not so hard on Brushy as then: but it disappointed a great many people, about going to the quarterly meeting. Uncle Joes folks had been fixing for it for three weeks and Prudence was also making grand preparations for the reception of company, and allmost every body was “fixing up” to go to the quarterly meeting; but on Saturday morning the clouds, which had been hanging Sullenly around for the past few days, began to let fall their “garnered fullness” which soon made many a face, I have no doubt, look as gloomy as they. The consequence of it all was, the “magnificent meeting” as Mrs [[Thos.?]] Hillin would have it, was a “Sublime failure”.
I would have [[deleted: went]] [[inserted: gone]] Sunday any how despite the mud and water if it had not been, the horses, on that particular morning took care to keep themselves, clear out of sight: none up but Jenny, our new nag and you know I could not go by myself. Mary Orr had been nearly all week making a new dress to wear, so she was highly disappointed. Ann Kelly had all of her ribbons in a box ready to start down here, so you may be sure there was a “tempest in the teapot;” there. The miss Bransons of [[four?]] mile got to uncle Joes before the rain commenced so y[[lost: edge]] see there were a few strangers there. The miss [[Farrars?]] of Chambers Creek were also up, also Mr Duate, who has re[[lost: end of word at edge]] his health, and intends returning to the army soon I must continue

07-037 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 37
07-037-P01
We were highly gratified, on tuesday evening last, by the arrival of Warren and Beck. Warren has about recovered from his sickness though he has not entirely regained his strength. They cannot stay long with us, on account of Warrens wanting to start back to the army about the first of next week. They will have to start home on Sunday next. We are very sorry of this, as we thought they would stay at least three or four weeks when they did come. But “to arms! to arms!” is the cry, and every man that can drag one foot after another must go. We have no late news from any where, every thing [[deleted: seems to be]] is a stand still in this way of news, but the war keeps going on there is no stop to that; and whatever raised such a hope of peace by the “first of March” and the “first of June” and the “first of July”; is more than I can tell. I have got out of all hopes of peace, soon. If Old Lincoln had ever meditated peace, he would not be enrolling his men from twenty to forty; and the South is not going to give it up, as long as they [[deleted: can]] muster a thousand men in my opinion.
Three O Clock P.M. Not feeling very well to day I have been trying to “snooze” a little and as I feel somewhat refreshed I will try to write some more, although I feel like I can't write any thing that would interest you. The ballance of the family are well and the health of the neighbourhood I believe is generally good, with the exception of Mrs Payne, who is now very low: it is feared she will not recover. Some of us will have to go over there to sit up to night. Sis Bell staid with us last night, the first time she has visited us since you left; which by the by is just four months ago to day. Four long months it seems to me more like a year. Lizzie Bell and Jennie have neither been here on a visit since you left They say they can't get time to come but they manage to get time to go every where else

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continues 07-036, followed by 07-038. Statements about conscription, Lincoln’s intentions and prospects for peace are the writer’s contemporary understanding and opinion.

07-038 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 38
07-038-P01
I will not quarrel with them about it, of course; for if they do not want to come I will not want them to: but it pains me to think, that people whom I have always considered as friends, to appear so distant: not so distant either when we meet, for the always appear friendly and ask nay, beg me to come to see them, but I cannot think people sincere when every thing is in word, and nothing in action.
But “with these few remarks” we will drop the subject and wander on, and perhaps we will strike something more interesting. Father finished planting his six acres of corn [[deleted: just]] last week, or rather [[deleted: he]] Walker did: and this fine rain on it, I think it will do well, if we can just get it worked. Perhaps you would like to hear how the ground is divided off. We will begin at the west end of the field. Mr Graves takes the ground worked last year by Penee Nave and Walker; then Mr Dawkins comes in he has fourteen acres which includes the dewberry patch then Uncle Alf takes a few acres I don't know the exact number about four or five though, I think: this brings us down to the wheat. Father has left some ground just west of your wheat where he intends sowing the hungarian grass, then comes the corn and from the corn to the house and from the house to the Graves ground is left uncultivated I think there is about ten acres left for the weeds.
This has been a beautifully clear day. The wind is from the South plenty warm this evening to have both doors open. The cotton wood trees have leafed out enough to give considerable shade. And just let me inform you the varmints are getting pretty thick. I went out to milk the other morning looked down in the bottom right south of the calf pen and saw some kind of an animal I could not tell whether a fox or wild cat and I did not follow it, to make out its particular title.

07-038-P02
[[separate block: inverted upper margin]]
Mother staid with Mrs Payne last night she is no better

07-039 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 39
07-039-P01
Friday 3rd. I got so sick yesterday evening, I had to drop my pen and quit writing. I feel right smartly better this morning and I think I will be well now. I wasnt very sick at first, but the medicine I took made me very sick.
The ballance are all well. Ellen has just come up to me and says tell Uncle George “just one more letter”.
I commenced telling you about the game yesterday evening. The deer have become allmost gentle; as I was going to the office the other day, I saw three, they circled around me about fifty yards off, held up their heads and looked at me as saucy as you please, while they trotted gently along. The turkeys appear to be very scarce this Spring; I have only heard one or two gobble yet: I saw a gang of six over the creek the other day, the only ones I have seen; directly afterwards Rob and his brotherinlaw Parks passed on down the creek after them, a gun awakened the echoes that evening, the first sound that had aroused them, for many a day.
I am very glad indeed, that the conscript let Rob off; for I consider him a good man, and very useful to the neighbourhood, besides, he never had any thing to do, in bringing on the present troubles; but alas many a poor fellow as innocent as he has to bear the trials and hardships in common with those that brought it on. But it is no use to talk about who brought it on, and did not now, for we are all into it: but a person cant help thinking about things: here is Graves and all of his family at home, and you off fighting for his negroes, a person can deny it looks hard: but let me not be ungrateful to Mr Graves, for he is the only one that interested himself about tending our ground, I should not have said the only one either, for Rob would have taken some I expect if Mr Graves had not.
I reckon I had better not ask you any more questions, as you were taken so heavily on account of my questions before. I think they were all put to it for something to talk about, to go to joking you about that. I wish you could get a good joke on that Capt. You can tell him old Mrs Partington heaved a sigh when she read he carried all of his wounded men out of the fray him self, and thought, “no [[deleted: doubt]] wonder the poor little delicate man fell down in the water, when that [[counchie?]] shoulder exclaimed Oh! my Susters [[separate block: side margin, continuing quotation]] if you dont take us away from here we will all be killed!!”

07-039-P02
[[separate block: inverted upper margin]]
You must excuse this letter if it partakes some of my sickness, for I do feel pretty bad this morning you need'nt tell Evans what Old Mrs Partington said unless you can run a good joke on him by it. With my love to you and Joda I remain Affectionately Lizzie

EDITORIAL NOTE: Final leaf of April 2–3 letter. In the sentence about Graves, “can deny” is retained as read although “cannot deny” might be expected. The joke uses a difficult phrase read tentatively as counchie shoulder; no exact meaning or corrected wording is supplied. The next sentence names Evans in connection with the joke. The quotation runs along the lower and side margins.

07-041-P01
In Little Room Jan 28th 1863
Dear Brothers Warren & George
I received your letter of the 18th yesterday at noon we ar so anxious to hear from you all some of us go to the Office Twice a week & ar most all ways there the day your letters come as they arive most invariable on Tuesday or Friday, rain or shine some one is there. It has been very rainy for the last 3 weeks it rained all day for 2 Sundays Then in the middle of the week besides. Though it has not affected the well at all I think the old well is beyond cure. Every body else's wells ar full. The creek is runing briskly. Wheat looks tolerable well considering the dry fall, the ground is very soft since so much rain & the little Snow. We had more rain than we have had since last Spring the hog-wallows are all full it looks as if the drouth was over. if it is I look for better times for War & famine go together, now if the famine is over wont the war be soon Oh! I hope so.
I heard to day Lincoln has been killed Shot while in his carriage. now I cant give credit to this but Then it may be so. I wish it may be if it would in any way bring the war to a close probable if another were in power Thing would take a turn for the better. better or worse I suppose we must put up with it. We have no late news from Ark. All well last account. [[Darnells?]] Reg. has started east of this River to Vicksburg whether they get across or not is uncertain the River being full of gunboats. Nashville is not retaken. Memphis is. [[Hamman?]] [[Brinn?]] & Loyd were killed in that fight several more wounded I have not learned their names. Thus falls one by one of our acquaintances. [[3?]] of the Lancaster Co. have been killed several others died, will half get back.
I got a letter from Beck the other day of the 10th they were all well getting finely she had not got any letters relative to the fight up to that time. Mr Evins has not been down yet after the corn [[lost: lower edge; overlapping view continues at 07-042]]

EDITORIAL NOTE: Beginning of Laura’s letter (signature at 07-047), physically inverted in scan. The lower portion is repeated and extended at 07-042. Reports about Lincoln and military movements are explicitly contemporary hearsay; the supposed killing of Lincoln in this January 1863 letter is a false rumor, not the later assassination. Names and the small numeral before Lancaster remain uncertain.

07-052-P01
Houston Jan 26th 1863
In reply to yours of 14th I will begin by saying that I am in a hurry and have but a little time to spare at the present as it is Sundown and after night I will not have an opportunity to write and I want to put this in the office so it will go up tomorrow. For several days we have had some very cold weather in this latitude and it has not yet run out yet no rain or Sleet however to incommode us this time. Our stove we enjoyed finely also the Society of our friends who called on us frequently.
Rations are about as [[deleted: usual]] usual this time of year we get plenty of Meal not quite of beef and nothing else. Soap Sugar Molasses Vinegar and such like articles are “played out.” We Still have some of “that” on hand yet but when the supply is exhausted we will have to fall back on No. one for supplies. This Evening Chas G went to [[Fox's?]] Soap factory to buy soap He enquired if we were soldiers and to what

1863

07-058-P02
Sunday morning: the wind is in the north it got there yesterday morning so I suppose by this time it has reached you. It is quite cloudy, but I do not think we will have rain to day. This is Fathers birth day: he is sixty two years old and enjoys better health than he has for years past, I suppose, on account of exercise. I will quit as I might run this into a “sister Jane of thousand words”. Affectionately Lizzie

07-058-P03
George you must excuse me for finishing my letter to Joda on your paper but as we presume that each of you see the others letters we think it dont make much difference. Our paper and envelops are getting quite scarce as Warrall failed to go to Cedar hill to get us more at the stated time so we have to do the best we can. Lizzie has written so much that I dont know what else to offer. I think you are pretty severe in your criticism of her letters, but perhaps it will be an advantage to her in the end as it may serve to spur her mental capacities which would otherwise have remained dormant. Take good care of yourself keep company with the intelligent and [[separate block: right margin, continuing sentence]] well disposed kiss little white Lily for me and don't forget [[deleted: illegible]] your Emmie and little Ted. Yours Sue

The statement that Father is sixty-two could support a February 15, 1801 birth date if this dating and the father’s identity are confirmed. It does not by itself identify his father or birthplace. The quoted sister Jane phrase is retained as read.

You must be sure to write to us when your clothes give out, socks as well as your other clothes, so that we can send you more.
I have counted it up and to night you are standing guard if if you are not sick. I expect you think of home right often when you get off in the cold with no one to talk to; but don't get homesick the time may be nearer than we anticipate, when we will have peace and you will all get to come home again. I do not recollect what Laura wrote, but I suppose from your letter, she must have presented rather a gloomy picture. If so I will just attribute it to the state of her mind on that occasion for you know, we all feel more gloomy at times than others. 07-062-P01
Sister Lizzie
Sabine March [[30th?]] /64. No 64
As the month is almost out I thought I had as well finish it off by writing a day or two sooner than usual, not that there is any thing interesting going on but to pass off time. Bad colds were [[illegible]] in this [[illegible]] for I have quite a [[severe?]] bad cold. Somehow go [[ill?]] with me in this latitude than they did in Ellis, the only reason I can assign for the difference is, the cold in this section is damper.
Don't yell too fast on the Peace question, everybody is perfectly cool in this country; don't look for peace until one side or the other is completely exhausted, and it will take some time to do that. Report came here yesterday to the effect that the Yankees had taken Sabine Town and a battery with equipment at that place. (cant vouch for the truth of it, though I think it is generally credited). Sabinetown is 125 miles above here on the Sabine river, and about 100 miles due West from Alex. Taylors Cavalry have been ordered to La and have gone. All is quiet here and the Weather very good; We did have a cool norther but that has blown over.
Four men deserted from Bickleys Co night before last and went to the blockade. Somehow some of the rebs still have hankering for Sea life. This last act continuing in the service for the war in their present organizations all between the ages of 18 & 45 is an “eye opener” and rather gives the lie to the universal reenlistment of the troops on the other side. Well every thing has been done that can be done and that is some satisfaction. Firstly. Every able bodied white male citizen of the Confederacy between the ages of 17–50 is hereby declared to be in the Military Service of the Confed. for the War! & c
Secondly. Persons owning 15 able bodied field hands on the 1st Jany 1864 are hereby exempt, provided such persons sell all surplus provisions raised Year to Year to the Govt at fixed prices, & bind themselves to furnish [[100?]] lbs Meat [[illegible]] hand

07-065 | manuscript

07-065-P01
No 51
Dear Sisters, Sabine Jany 11th 64
Another week has passed quite disagreably, considerable sleet fell the other night, the ground froze tolerably hard, the wind damp and chilly and all together disagreable. Today is cloudy and threatening rain, mud is abundant. It is all a joke about this Latitude being warm in the winter time it is not as cold as it is in Ellis but then the cold is damp thus making it more disagreable than it would be if it was dry. After all things considered we are faring very well for soldiers and should not complain. It is much more pleasant to be quartered in houses than it is to lie out without tents as they have to do out about Lavaca. Of beef and bread we get enough to live on tolerably well, fare we [[illegible]] a great deal better than some others.

07-065-P02
Late advices from the east are discouraging, the yankees are jubilant and the rebels downcast, everything looks dark for the Confederacy, our armies are in bad condition and the enemy Vice Versa, our men all want to go home, the yankees say they intend to reenlist (See Tel, 8th Jany). The militia are very home sick and intend going home as soon as their six months is out, go where it leads. 50 desertions have occurred from our batt since the last big scout in Dec, it is reported that some of them have been taken but I am inclined to disbelieve the report, it came in rather a crooked way. The Davis Guards have continued to desert some eight or ten having gone to the yankees. As a Co they were moved by harsh treatment, for some slight offence one of them has been balled and chained and they say Magruder promised them that they should never be punished in so degrading a manner. They petitioned him to remit the sentence of this man, and he [[illegible: faded bottom line]]

07-066 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 66
07-066-P01
Since the first, one or three more have been balled and chained and they threaten if they are not treated better they will give up the fort to the yankees the next time they come along. So much for so much, what the foregoing is worth remains to be seen, if the “Paddies” carry out their threat it will be a serious affair.

07-066-P02
Great dissatisfaction exists in the Batt which threatens serious results, and if somebody dont back out some one will get hurt. About three months ago two men (not in Co C) missed roll call. The roll was called some fifteen minutes earlier than usual and before the drum beat. The orderly sergeant ordered them to carry some guns as a punishment for their absence, this they refused to do because the roll was called before the proper time. They were arrested and tried for disobedience of orders and sentenced to wear a barrel shirt [[20 Dy?]] [[inserted: twenty two hours each day]] and then ten days solitary confinement on bread and water alone. On the barrels was marked their names and the words “disobedience of orders and fatigue duty”. Yesterday the attempt was made to put the barrels on them when some of their Co came out with their guns to resist the enforcement of the order. The barrels proved to be too small and larger ones were procured by this morning. In the mean time however Col Griffin ordered the mutineers to be put in the guardhouse, this they resisted and a great many of the Batt promised to sustain them. This morning they left camps and went out in the country, thus abandoning their arms and cause. Col Griffin made a speech to the Batt and told them that if they resisted the decree of the court martial he would arrest all concerned for mutiny, and if he could not do it with what men were here he would report the fact to Magruder who would use every means in his power to arrest and punish them to the extent of the law. [[Shriver?]] as it would be mutiny to resist the order

07-067 | manuscript

07-067-P01
and the original parties having [[carried?]] it all quietly knocked under and allowed them to wear the barrels. Co C showed more disposition to mutiny than any of the others. Of the others or the men that came out with their guns to resist the order yesterday the Col declared it his intention to arrest if possible and punish. I suppose however they have abandoned the post a thing I would do if I were in similar circumstances, but I hope the time may never come when I will have to mutiny. Such rigorous punishments for such slight offences is having a very demoralizing effect on the army, it has caused directly near twenty desertions and it will cause a great many more. Griffin stands at least forty degrees below zero in the estimation of his command, he is despised for being so precise and military in his conduct, he governs men by the force of military law and not by anything like mildness: he treats them pretty much in the same manner an overseer treats his negroes, never has any thing to say to them only when he wants something done, this is the character of the man and I suppose he cant help it; but one thing I have learned never to get in a regt again commanded by a military man. All has quietly flowed over and it is to be hoped we will have peace in the command for the future.

07-067-P02
I received your letter of Dec 19 the other day, and in answer to your query about Warren I can only say he is as big a fool as ever, he is like an old hard shell Baptist you cant convince [[inserted: him]] of any thing he dont want to be convinced of. Nearly everybody else is disgusted, and in my opinion the Confederacy cant last much longer unless some great change takes somewhere, something must [[deleted: turn out]] turn up that will change the whole aspect of affairs and that shortly or its “up” or “out”. Besides what I have already said I believe there is nothing new or interesting.

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continuation of 07-066. Opening syntax and the reading “carried” are uncertain; the family version flags this rather than silently repairing it. 07-068 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 68
07-068-P01
From the reading of late official documents I learn that the impressment act is not working up to their expectations, apparently more dissatisfaction is expressed than was expected. Maybe Congress will repeal it, it would be a good plan I expect for taking things from private individuals by main force is a bad plan, if the people are not willing to support a government it is bound to fall inspite of all efforts made by a few to the contrary. If the people dont think enough of the country to save it themselves the policy is a poor one to try to force them to it.

07-068-P02
The defeat at Chattanooga you will see will turn out pretty much as I predicted, it will cost the Confederacy Thirty Thousand men, and three fourths of them will be lost by prestige; look at the admissions made by the Houston Tel. Abe’s last proclamation is a [[tall news?]] document. As fast as the yankees get possession of the country the people will take the oath as prescribed by the proclamation. ’Tis a tempting bait to have security of persons and property guaranteed simply by taking an oath, which can be broke in two minutes after an opportunity is offered.

07-068-P03
Morgans escape was a pretty “cute” thing and no doubt John will trouble the yankees a sight now yet. Dont you think that “[[View-au-Sie?]]” colors his pieces pretty highly, Somehow or other sensation pieces dont rate as high as they used to. &c &c.

07-068-P04
With the slightest imaginable hope for peace this summer I remain affectionately George.

EDITORIAL NOTE: Conclusion of January 11, 1864 letter, 07-065–068. Criticism of impressment, military losses, oaths, and newspaper reporting are George’s opinions. The name or pseudonym near the end and the phrase describing the proclamation remain uncertain. The letter does not establish the predicted casualty total as historical fact.

07-070-P01
Sister Lizzie, Manhassett May 10th 64 [[illegible: letter number]]
The time since our last writing has been [[replete?]] with events of interest, and I suppose that before this reaches you you will have obtained the outlines of the news, so I will fill at once with the details. Last Wednesday night we got marching orders for Calcasieu, at sundown we struck and went as far as town, there we were supplied with three days rations of Crackers and bacon, each ones outfit then consisted of one blanket canteen three days rations musket and sixty rounds of ammunition. We were then ordered to go to sleep and in the long reeds [[illegible: several words crossed by show-through]] and commenced cursing the [[illegible]]. At daylight all arose and took up the line of march.

07-070-P02
The first six miles lay across a bog marsh over which [[scores?]] of Stock had passed when wet and the walking was rendered more difficult by the rank grass. Here a great blunder was made by marching too far and fast without rest, several gave out to lie down in the first six miles. Our road now lay along a sandy ridge through a thin settlement where refreshment &c water could be obtained in abundance. At the end of the point 20 miles we stopped for the artillery to come up. At four oclock the [[round?]] was resumed and about a half an hour by sun we passed the last house on the peninsula, yet to go was some 18 miles; the Sgts we thought it [[knew?]] and for some 6 miles the Capt and [[illegible]] were moving constantly. About midnight we reached [[Oyster?]] Bay which led to the [[illegible]], we snatched an hours sleep while the Sappers and [[illegible]] built the bridge. It was six miles yet to the gunboats, and three to water every canteen was empty [[cursing?]] was [[dry?]] and very grainy too. When we reached the well there was nothing to bring water with. So we had to march on with no prospect

07-071-P02
Seeing the confused state of the men the officers tried to get them in line, but no sooner had the command “Guide Right” been given than all [[deleted: illegible]] crowded over against the right guide and were getting directly between the battery and boat (the boat had not yet opened fire, we afterward learned the first intimation they had of our approach was the battery playing on them). The officers then commanded “Guide left” the crowd surged off to the left in a bunch. Seeing every man was pretty much his own commander, and every one had lost his place in ranks I concluded I would be my own general, I let the crowd go but continued forward in ranging from behind and before, for I knew the crowd would draw the grape and the shot and shell passed a few feet over me. I kept my eyes on the muzzles of the cannon in front and whenever one flashed I would fall a little quicker than I had ever performed the maneuver before. I kept on this way

07-075 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 75
07-075-P01
Dear Sister, Manhassett July 10th/64 — No [[77?]]
Your letter of June 26th came to hand last friday; and found us all hearty. Times are dry though we had a good rain the other day. We contrive to live pretty well for the times, had roasting ears and tomato soup for dinner dont you think that will do very well for a Reb? especially when it is obtained twice or thrice a week, we could live a good deal better if somebody would run in a load of garden seeds from some foreign port. Vegetables degenerate so rapidly here that in the course of two or three years they run out. I have been told beets will not go to seed here, and cabbage will only head the first year. There is no kind of vegetable here that is the same to be the natural production of the soil. Melons and grapes grow finely, I have seen tolerably good corn cotton and tobacco, potatoes sweet and Irish grow finely. Irish are about extinct, the people depended on getting seed from the north but the blockade shut down on that dependence and left them without. If I owned a place here I would have a vineyard. I think the soil here is well adapted to the growth of all kinds of grapes, mustang grapes grow spontaneously, the “French” grow pretty well in gardens. This is a fine country barring the musquitoes.

07-075-P02
For the last three or four weeks we have loafed around camps and done nothing but this week a few more lessons will have to be taken at the big guns. Artillery drill is easier learned than infantry, but I dont like the way they rattle in a fight, they are what draw the balls bombs and Shrapnel. The latter is a spherical case filled with musket balls one side of the case is very thick the other quite thin, the thick side is put in the gun next the powder, the thin as a matter of course goes in front. When they explode the entire charge of balls is thrown forward scattering like an old blunderbuss and properly directed will kill and cripple all the men at a gun. [[illegible: concluding phrase; words “our cannon and” and “at Calcasieu” visible]]

07-076-P01
For [[lawing?]] for angry Rebs [[Morrow?]] received some compensation but to what extent, according to the nature of the cases, I do not know. Almost every kind of cases came before him as to him another, some Lo Co [[gians?]] had themselves proved legally dead to avoid conscription. Everything between this and desertion came into his line of business. If men did not have to stay into and come into the service but very few would be in the ranks now. I confidently believe that if every man were discharged that would come in, in two months the yankees would be in every hamlet and village of the South. It is strange how men can be made do anything but they can be driven about by the leaders just like an ox driver drives his team about. News from Va is to the effect that Grant has been checked in his onward movements and that he has gone to fortifying and that he will have to take Richmond by siege. Nothing but from [[Johnson?]] and Sherman.

07-076-P02
The other day we were inspected by an officer of Magruders staff a Capt with more conceit than brains and sense of both. There was so much grease on the guns he got his hands dirty which no doubt caused him a good deal of trouble, he presented quite a Dirty appearance and after inspection was over the boys began discussing his merits loud enough for him to hear. Some said he was [[illegible]] others Dutch others something else finally deciding however that he was Dutch and did not understand his business. He wanted to know of Evans if he allowed his men to talk that way. Evans who had not been paying attention to what was being said replied “yes he generally allowed them to say what they pleased”. He replied that would have to report us well armed and drilled and presenting a fine military appearance but in a very bad state of discipline. That chap wont want to inspect this Comp again shortly. A great many inspecting officers come around to see what we have on hand in the way of clothing &c and make reports to Hd Qrs but I never could see as it ever done us any good. Fayette is inclined to poke fun at me in the “Belle Lettres” department, However I think I keep ahead of “Websters Unabridged”. Affectionately George.

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continuation of 07-075. Opening legal-business passage, the Lo Co label, and one reported army commander’s name are uncertain. “Belle Lettres” is the wording as read. The writer’s views of compulsory service and reports about military movements are retained as his statements.

Brother George

07-102-P01
Sunday Dec. 11th ’64
Brother George
I suppose you have become domiciled again in camps by this time and perhaps the monotony of some lonely hours may be relieved by a line from me. We are all tolerably well my own health is not very good but now that winter has set in I hope to improve.
It has been pretty cold here since last wednesday and people are busy killing hogs as it happens though my chance for hog meat is pretty slim owing doubtless to the absence of the only one who was competent to take care of them.
My mind has been occupied lately with an idea of moving I think if I can possibly make the eddy I will leave here in the spring and go down on the Nueces

EDITORIAL NOTE: Letter continues on the following scans. “Make the eddy” is retained as written; in context she is considering whether she can manage the move, not announcing that it has occurred.

Norvell aims to haul forty bales in the spring and as long as he must be absent from home he had as well try to make it pay. He has four teams now on the road or I suppose at Brownsville now hauling thirty bales at nine cents per lb from San Antonio

07-108 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 108
07-108-P01
I received a letter from home yesterday morning dated March 24th all wear well at that time no news of importance I Shall stay here tweleve or ten days yet before I Start to Brownsville. J. H. Collins has a yoke of oxen runing on Danville I want you to see him and know if he will sell them and lets me know his price and if it is not to mutch I will send you the money to by them for me
Give my best respects to J. M. Bell & Warren Also to Collins write to me
I am
[[N. B.?]] Winniford

EDITORIAL NOTE: Conclusion of 07-107. Signature initials remain tentative. “Tweleve or ten” is retained in its original order. Danville is the visible place name; no location beyond the letter is inferred.
