08-094 | letter, first page
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 5 - Daybook of N.L. Douglas.pdf | PDF scan page 94
08-094-P01
Lewis County Tenn May the 25 [[1854?]]
Miss [[S.?]] Douglap
I now take my pen in hand to let you know that I am well at this time and hope that when thes comes to hand it will find you well I received your letter a few days ago which brought date April the 23 which gave me plesure to here that you were well [[deleted: illegible word]]

08-094-P02
I am not maried yet and dont no when I will be there is more prospects now than when [[deleted: illegible word]] I wrote to you last but I can tell you when it will be in about three years yet I have give my self away to one in [[Raugherford?]] and expect to waite for him I received a letter from him the same day that I received yours

08-094-P03
When you go to get maried send me word and make hast and get maried but dont quit writing to me for you have wrote to me before I love you as well as if you were here to me for we were raised up to gether whilst we were loved children but we are now a great ways apart but I hope we will not forget onenother untill we are taken away [[inserted: by death]]

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continues on 08-095, signed Sarah E. Barr. Year and addressee initial are uncertain. 08-096-P01
Murfreesboro Rutherford County Tenn June 5th 1854
Mr N. L. Douglass my old and tried friend your letter dated April the 25th [[inserted: came to hand on the 27th of May]] enclosing an eighty acre land warrant regularly transferred, with the request that I would dispose of it to the best advantage and pay the proceeds to Mr G. A. Sublett, which request was attended to with as much punctuality as the nature of the case would admit of. which you will learn from his receipt which you will find herein enclosed. I sent the warrant to Nashville, and ninety dollars is the highest price that can be commanded in that market, the speculators commanding ninety three in New York. I have reserved a copy of the receipt to guard against miscarriage or other accidents

08-096-P02
By the by our old friend Sublett continues in bad health I think his constitution is perfectly prostrate and that he never will regain any thing like general health again. I would here remark that the Cholera made its debut upon the City of Nashville on or about the 26th of last month, and also at several places in this County, more especially the west end of this County adjoining Davidson. There have been fifteen or twenty died in Nashville in two or three days when it first broke out, and also about the same number in this County, but it has some what abated (the weather having become more favorable to health) still there is a spirit of apprehension resting upon the bosom of the community

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continues on 08-097 and 08-098, signed Hicks. Insertion is placed after the letter date. Reports of health, deaths and prices are the writer’s contemporary claims, not independently verified statistics.

Anderson Ott has sold out his little farm near this place, and has bought a farm of about 150 acres ten miles South-east of Town on the Manchester turnpike. He and his family are all well. Nat. Ott is carrying on a shop, but his health is very delicate, last Spring twelve months he had a dangerous attack of Hemorage of the lungs, and a slight recurrence of it this Spring my opinion is that he is bleeding internally working at his trade. His family are all well at present

08-097-P02

Dear Sir
I saw Esq Jetton on yesterday and he shewed a letter from you dated 24th May last—In which, amongst many other inquiries, you wished to know where the battle of Stones River was fought. Who of our Citizens was Killed &c Now I will endeavour to post you as well as I can, although I have never been over the battle field—the right Wing of the Yanky army rested on the Franklin Road about McCullochs old residence & the line extended down the river a short distance below Old Uncle Billy Mitchell place, the Center resting on the Turnpike a little beyond [[Cavins?]] residence—The monument which they have erected to the Yanky Slain is about 2 or 3 hundred yards West of [[Cavins?]] Cotton Gin, that used to Stand on the right hand of the Turnpike & about Opposit his residence—and a little below that on the old [[Menife?]] place is the National Cemetery between the Rail Road & Turnpike & [[deleted: a short distance of the]]

08-117-P03
You also wish to know who of the Citizens of Town, or County was Killed, I only recollect a few names of our Citizens the first was Fred James eldest Son of Allen James and a Son of Madison Smith, & a Mr Samuel Marley who was raised near Middleton, Albert [[Abernathy?]], Grand Son of Mrs Clementine Hall—these are all that I now recollect that were Killed in the battle at this place—There was a good many other Citizens of Town & County Killed in other fields (Viz) a Son of John N black at Shilow—Walter Wendel Son of D D Wendel Killed at Perryville Ky—Saml Ransom Son of John—Richd Sublett Son of E A Sublett at Petersburg—John Wrather Son of our John Wrather the Printer at [[Murfreesboro?]]—George Lee Parker Son of Isaac Killed at [[continues]]

08-117-P04
[[separate block: marginal postscript, partly cropped]] [[lost: beginning]] Son is living—Mr Mosby request me to say that Mr Nance was up a few days since with his baby girl & there is none [[lost: edge]] & wife all well
[[D W S?]]

08-118-P01
Chickamauga—Colo John Butler Son of Thomas O Butler Killed Perryville Ky—& a Young Man by the name of Wharton who Came here from Virginia Since you left this Country Killed at Perryville—& my Second Son Robt, was Killed at Marietta Georgia—the above is all of the Killed that I can think of in this Town & Country—and now I will give you a list of Old Citizens that have died in the last few years from natural Causes (to wit) Henry D Jamison—Burrill Gannaway—Elisha Williams—Love & Moses Reeves—William Snell—Wm F Lytle—W D Cannon—Thomas O Butler—Silas Tucker—Lewis Tucker—Revd Wm Eagleton—Wm Brick—Wm M Fadden—Henry Hall—Benjamin Clayton—Benjamin Rucker and our fellow townsman Reuben Ballis was Killed 3 or 4 Weeks Since, by attempting to pull down a Cabin that he had bought, & intended moving

08-118-P02
our town & County have been greatly damaged by the two Armies, they destroied all the timber for miles around burnt all the rails for 3 or 4 miles in all directions burnt & pulled down at least 50 houses in town & of this number was the Old Presbyterian Church, destroied the fence around the grave, broke tombstones & desecrated the grave Yard generally, Sent Some of the Citizens through their lines & took possession of their houses & Stole, & Sent off, their beding, & furniture—in short they were a Set of Vandals—Esqr Jetton wishes me to Say to you that he will Send you a Check in a few days for one hundred dollars—John D Alexander is in town, rd. your letter, & request me to Send you his best respects & Say he will write to you Very Soon—and Wm Brick has promised to write to you Soon—and Robt S Burney, is editor of the Murfreesboro Monitor promised to Send you a Copy of his paper Soon—I encouraged him to do so as I thought you would take it as a Special favour—you will please write to me, whenever you feel like writing & tell me all about your part of Texas how you are getting along & of the products & all else you can think of, which will interest your old friend

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continuation of 08-117, rotated 180 degrees. 08-138 | manuscript copy of legal provisions
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 5 - Daybook of N.L. Douglas.pdf | PDF scan page 138
08-138-P01
Sec 33. Where the wife dies, her husband surviving, administration [[inserted: is unnecessary]] except as to any separate estate which may have belonged to her. The husband continues to have the same power of disposition over the community property which he possessed during the continuance of marriage. But he shall be required to return an inventory and appraisement of all such property; and to file a bond, signed [[deleted: Signed]] by one or more sureties, to be approved by and payable to the district clerk of the county; in an amount equal to the value of the whole of the community property; to the effect that he will faithfully administer the same, and pay over one half of the surplus after the payment of the debts with which the whole is properly chargeable, to such person or persons as shall be entitled to receive it.

08-138-P02
Sec 34 The husband is liable to be called to account at any time after one year from the date of the bond.

08-138-P03
Sec 35. Such bond is suable, recoverable, and in every other respect the same as the bond of an administrator.

08-138-P04

08-152 | letter
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 5 - Daybook of N.L. Douglas.pdf | PDF scan page 152
08-152-P01
Austin Texas April 10/69
N L Douglass Esq
Waco Texas
Sir
The Draft was received by the Comptroller this morning. It came yesterday but when we called for it the mail had not been distributed, hence we did not get it. I have endorsed the draft in accordance with the authority you gave me and the draft will be sent to Houston for collection. As soon as we hear from it I will send you the Comptrollers receipt for the amount. You need not give yourself any uneasiness about it. I will attend to it and you shall be troubled no further. With the best wishes for your safe return to your home & family I remain
Your Friend
Joseph Spence

08-152-P02
I will write to you at Red oak in a few days
Spence

EDITORIAL NOTE: Date is written April 10/69. The draft amount is not repeated here, so it is not assumed to be the Norton payment or any particular deposit without further evidence.

08-164 | letter
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 5 - Daybook of N.L. Douglas.pdf | PDF scan page 164
08-164-P01
Quincy Tenn
June 5th 67
N. L. Douglass — Sir — I recd your verry Short epistle, accompanied by a Recept a Short time Since — In this I would ask you a Single question — Did you In any way assist In freeing the Negro Sam? I write this to know the certainty, you know, and you will please answer the question — if you answer In the affirmative I will forward to you your recept. If not, I will take grate pains to forward your money — I am verry good for the amt Claimed —

08-164-P02
Now Sir, You & I are getting old, and Soon our earthly Interests will [[deleted: have]] be at an end, Consequently I dont want to do wrong — Now all I mean in this is, If you assisted In taking my property from me, you can get your money by ligal process — If not, I will take pleasure If forwarding It to you —

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continues on 08-165. The final If may be a slip for in; direct wording is retained. The letter’s claim of ownership and accusation are the writer’s, not editorial findings.

08-167 | oath of office
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 5 - Daybook of N.L. Douglas.pdf | PDF scan page 167
08-167-P01
Oath of Office.
I N L Douglas do solemnly swear that I have never voluntarily borne arms against the United States since I have been a citizen thereof; that I have voluntarily given no aid countenance council or encouragement to persons engaged in armed hostility thereto; that I have neither sought nor accepted nor attempted to exercise the functions of any office whatever under [[deleted: the]] any authority or pretended authority in hostility to the United States; that I have not yielded a voluntary support to any pretended government authority power or constitution within the United States hostile or inimical thereto; And I do further swear that to the best of my knowledge and ability I will support and defend the constitution of the United States against all enemies foreign and domestic, that I will bear true faith and allegiance to the same, that I take this obligation freely without any mental reservation or purpose of evasion and that I will well and faithfully discharge the duties of the office on which I am about to enter So help me God.

EDITORIAL NOTE: The reverse is labelled January 1868 (08-166). The oath names N. L. Douglas in its opening, but this scan shows no separate signature, witness, attestation or specific office. It cannot by itself prove that an official administered or accepted the oath. Original council retained.

09-002 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 2
09-002-P01
Rutherford Co Tennessee April 18th 1852
Dear dauhter I received your Letter with Rebeccas dated October 18 1851 it come to hand in due time I would have answered it but I thought I would get another as soon as Mr Andrews got there—and I have bin waiting all this time and has got none
You wish me to [[deleted: illegible]] write often as I know by myself how glad I am to get one yes I am glad from my very hart to hear from you all—I am glad to hear that Susana wes Baptized I hope she will do good that she be rich in good works ready to distribute willing to Communicate laying up in store for herself a good foundation against the time to Come that she may lay hold [[deleted: illegible]] on eternal life
My sister Betsey is no more she died the 26 of january she suffered greatly she was [[tapt?]] 7 times she Lived 9 days on a little snow and snow water it was all she wanted she was very willing to die there [[inserted: fe]] ll a big snow on the 18 of january I visited her all I could while she was sick I was there by her when she died—I heard from you all by john Cock he said you was all well but Mr Douglass I am sorry to hear of his affliction I wish he could take care of himself and get well—I do not know how you can do there where every thing is so scearce and so dear—I [[deleted: illegible]] would like to hear whether the few things I sent you by Mr Andrews was damaged or not in cashing if the peafowl feathers went safe
[[separate block: margin]] Quoted from Timothy [[1st?]] [[6?]]. 18 verse

09-006 | manuscript

09-006-P01
Woodbury Cannon County Tenn
June 18th 1852.
Mr N L Douglas.
Dear Sir, I understand that Lewis Jetton wrote to you concerning the Death of Mother, though he did not state to you the particular incidents connected with that solemn unexpected and lamentable event, My dear Mother is no more; She departed this life on the 6th of May last; After having lived to the age of nearly Three Score and Ten years, and passing through the trials and vissicitudes of life with that patience, exercise and Christian deportment that characterize and distinguish her to a hight that many do not reach, in the paths of rectitude Morality and religion, She at last goes down in peace and quietude to the silent Tomb of the grave ready and prepared to take her Flight to the Mansions of Heaven in the Eternal Kingdom of God on the Morning of the resurrection.

EDITORIAL NOTE: Letter continues on 09-007–009, signed S. J. Goodloe and addressed to N. L. Douglas. Wrapper 09-010 expands the writer to Sam J. Goodloe and explicitly identifies the deceased mother as Rebecca Goodloe. “Nearly three score and ten” means nearly seventy.

I being

09-013 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 13
09-013-P01
The Pleasures of Memory.

09-013-P02
How often our minds revert [[inserted: pleasures]] to by gone days. Pleasures that were impressed upon our minds before we knew the cares of this world, never to be effaced by the corrosive hand of Time.
It is true, our minds are often burdened with the cares and perplexities of life, and we feel there is nothing bright to look upon; when all at once some familiar sound, a silvery voice, breaks the stillness of our hearts, and calls us back to some cherished scene of the past.
We think of the dear ones at home, whose loving hands were ever ministering to our wants, and whose guardian influence [[deleted: was]] ever directing our footsteps through the uneven scenes of life.

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continues through 09-015. Opening insertion “pleasures” has an awkward position; preserved rather than silently reconstructing the sentence. No signature or date appears on these three pages, and authorship is not established by the wrapper describing Emily’s separate song.

09-014-P01
We think of Home, that sacred spot where have been passed the happiest hours of life.
It matters not how drear the spot
How proud or poor the home
Love still retains some deathless chains
That bind the heart to home.

09-014-P02
We think of the surroundings of this home; the many happy hours spent in roaming over the broad prairies gathering the many colored flowers which was then the hith of our ambition. And again how much delight we would take in wandering along the mosscovered banks of the beautiful streams which were nearest us forgetful of Times rapid flight.

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continuation of 09-013. The four verse lines are set apart in the manuscript. “Hith” is retained as written, evidently meaning height in context.

09-015 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 15
09-015-P01
Let us think for a moment of the pleasures realized in after time, when we are old enough to attend Sunday school; how happy is each heart on entering the school room, as they crowd round their teacher in eagerness to learn sacred lessons from the holy Scriptures.
With what implicit confidence they look into their teachers face, and how indellibly his instructions are impressed upon their minds,
These scenes are permanently impressed upon my mind and I can imagine after our earthly race is almost run, we can truly say
There are moments in life [[inserted: that]] we never forget,
Which brighten and brighten, as time steals away;
They give a new charm to the happiest lot,
And shine on the gloom of the lonliest day.

09-018 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 18
09-018-P01
Columbus Oct. 24. 1855
Mrs Douglas
My Dear old friend
This evening I have determined to do what I have long wished to do, but not knowing your address (untill recently), I hope you will excuse me. I have just returned from Tennessee our old native place, There I learned your whereabouts. While there I saw Mrs Sam Davis who delivered a message sent by her husband I was more than happy to hear of your wellfare and future prospects, May you live long and be happy is the wish of my heart, and believe me my dear friend, there is none that feels more deeply interested for you and yours, than your humble servant. Well Polly (for so I am wont to speak) we both have had many troubles and trials to contend with since we parted, but it is all for our good if we love the Lord, I have long since learned that all things earthly are transitory and that this is not my abiding place, but look for a city whose maker and builder is God, My heart and Treasure is There, I have no cause to murmur, My health is fine, weigh 144. When I was in Tennessee I saw your sisters Mrs Jones and Mrs Nance, Doca was on a visit looks very thin, so does Julia, I did not see

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continues on 09-019–020, signed Miriam Stevenson. She calls Tennessee their old native place; this refers to writer and addressee, not independently to N. L. Douglas’s birthplace. Weight reproduced without supplying a unit not explicitly written. Doca/Dora name spellings vary across pages.

09-021 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 21
09-021-P01
Columbus March 29th. 1856
Dearest Mrs Douglass
After so long a delay It is with much pleasure that I acknowledge the receipt of your truly welcome letter. We have had a very cold and disagreeable winter, consequently great irregularity in our mails. but now the weather is pleasant I will venture to send my type, not because I thought it of much importance to any one, but I wish to live in your memory, and may be so you have forgotten my exact contour. If so, it will recall by gone days. yes this is me in my 48th year, weighing 145 and as youthful as when 19 (that is in my feelings and disposition
My health is fine except a slight touch of that fashionable disease, Neuralgia which knots me up a little at times. I am still teaching but think now that this is my last session, I am getting tired of confinement, I should like very much to travel if I were not a coward, but I must confess that water and steam affect my nerves so as to produce very unpleasant feelings.

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continues on 09-022. “Type” refers to the likeness being sent; the specific photographic process is not stated. Age and weight are retained as written. This letter describes a portrait but does not prove that the image survives among the supplied scans.

09-022 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 22
09-022-P01
I am truly rejoiced to learn of [[inserted: your]] wellfare and also of your childrens, they are all dear to me, because they are yours. & I would be happy to see you all but cannot now promise my self the pleasure of ever doing so But time nor absence can ever efface from memory the pleasant recollections of youthful days. No they are as green spots in my recollection that time nor distance will ever obliterate.
I received a letter from Sister Lou not long since, she says that your Cousin Tompson Wright was married to Miss [[Bowen?]] and that Virginia McKnight, (Williams wife) was dead. My friends here are all well, and desire to be remembered to your family. Say to Mr. D. I appreciate his good wishes, and kind regards and return them four fold.
My love to my dear Cousins James and Cynthie I do remember [[inserted: them]] fondly, and desire to be remembered by them. Please let me hear from you soon. My best wishes attend all that relates to you and yours, now farewell my dear kind friend farewell. May the Lord bless and protect you through life comfort you in death, and receive you in Heaven is the prayer of your friend. Miriam Stevenson.

Columbus July 6th 1856
My Dear kind friend Mrs Douglas
Your favor of May the 26 came safe to hand and found a warm reception, I was amused at the idea of your thinking that there had been a mistake perhaps in the picture. I do assure you that it is my own dear self, I had a head dress on of mohair with 3 curls on each side, My dress is of rich brocade, blue and brown, but the colors did not Take, I rejoice to learn of your [[deleted: illegible]] health and prospects. When I call to mind the many pleasant hours we have spent together it spreads a gloom over my feelings to know that [[inserted: they]] can never be recalled. But we must not permit the recollections of the past cast a shadow upon the future.
My health is pretty good, I shall leave for the country soon and remain 2 months, the warm season is not pleasant here

09-025 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 25
09-025-P01
It is very pleasant to get out and breathe the pure country atmosphere O I long to be off. I have been closely confined for 10 months but now I am free once more.
Well, having just returned from Church I will finish my letter. We had no preaching to day as our preacher is sick, but it is our practice to attend to the ordinances of the Lords house preacher or not, this we never neglect, and Oh that all could see and Appreciate their liberties as they ought, Then we should [[inserted: see]] Christians meeting together to sing, praise, and give thanks, rejoicing in the commandments of our Lord and Saviour. My dear friend this to me is the greatest pleasure of my life, I feel under many obligations to my Heavenly Father for his goodness to me particularly since I have been living in the South, circumstances have been peculiarly favourable to Christianity. You know that I was persecuted and shuned and sneered at on account of my faith and practice in my early career, but I always did and do now rejoice that I am counted worthy to be made partaker of his sufferings, who suffered so much for me.

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continuation of 09-024. Statements about past persecution and the South’s religious climate are Miriam’s personal testimony. No specific denomination or persecutor is named here.

09-028 | manuscript

09-028-P01
Wardville June 3d 1856
Dear Sister
I have recd. and read with much pleasure your kind favor of the 20th Ult.
I was surprised a little at first, but upon a thought I was surprised that I was surprised at all. For what is more to be expected than that we should often think of & write to each other. It is surprising that we never have before. As for me to forget you or to love you less, with the lapse of Time, & the change of circumstances the thing is simply impossible! for all my recollections of the past are inseperably connected with you.
Back to the extreme limit to which my memory stretches; you were the constant and almost only playmate of my early childhood and still onward through boyhood and youth and up to full Maturity you were my companion how then can or could we cease to cherish a warm and steady affection for each other
No, other ties may be formed—other friendships decay—but ours is part and parcel of our very lives, an affection [[inserted: that]] [[roots not low?]] in the clay.
I am well, and that is about all that I have to write about myself for nothing occurs to me that would interest you

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continues on 09-029–030, where the writer signs W. Douglas and names the recipient Rebecca Winnifrid. Metaphorical phrase near the bottom remains tentative. The initial is not expanded to a forename.

09-029 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 29
09-029-P01
these hard times. We had a greatdeal of wet weather this spring but it has been quite dry for some 3 weeks and rain is much needed.
The prospect for corn is pretty good wheat is nowhere in this country
I have recd. a letter from Henry by the same Mail that brought yours, he was well but times are dull with him too, & like me I think he is a little unsettled in his mind about his future course.
You seem a little horrified at the idea of my going to California; you need not be I think—for men, & better than yours, are & are going there. Every man of intelligence that I have ever conversed with who has seen California speaks highly of it as a Country. Many advise me to go & some are going the second time, with their families
I find it impossible to rise above a mere hand-to-mouth living in Texas, without the practice of the most stringent dealings & economy. Things that find place neither in my nature, nor my philosophy. Why then should I be so closely bound to Texas when I am already separated effectually, and hopelessly from you and all others, who love me.
If there is a better place why not find it Why not enjoy the best of a little world like this, when even that best, is bad enough
I do not think of any sudden acquirement

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continuation of 09-028. “Men, & better than yours” is retained as read. This passage states a proposed migration and its economic motivation; it does not establish that the journey occurred.

Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 47
09-047-P01
[[obscured: county name]] Co, Tenn
20th Apl [[1862?]]
Mr [[J.?]] D Orr
Dear Sir
Your very welcome letter of 28d March Came to hand yesterday,—found all in usual health. wife rather feeble, health generally good. We were very sorry to hear of James Sickness and hope he has before this time, So far recovered as to be able to come home,—We know Something of parents anxiety for a Sick Son away from home, and can truly Simpathize with you—
I am much pleased with the Spirit of your letter, and have in It expressed my Sentiments in refference to this unholy war waged against people who have never wronged a Yankey in no matter whatever while they cannot Say the Same of us. So Im In for everlastingly Separating from Such people. we now only [[obscured]] them to return to their homes and let us alone, thats all, and If they fail to do so many of their vile bodies will find a Southern home & by & by—Altho we have met with several disasters on the waters yet I feel encouraged, all seem to be satisfied that when they leave the waters we will make them bite the dust—
The roar of heavy ordinance is so common now as to attract but little attention, altho thers been none nearer than the Mis river. The enemy have possession of that river as far down as to Fort Pillow. that fortifycation is at Randolph opposite Covington the County cite of Tipton Co. I am told Its a strong place, but I dont know whether we will be able to hold It or not but I recon they will have a pretty lively time passing that point with their Gun boats I hear very heavy guns in that direction ever few [[obscured]] but cant learn any results [[obscured]] to get news as

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continues through 09-049, with an additional message on 09-050. County name obscured; recipient’s first initial and year tentative. The final year digit is ambiguous, but the body’s wartime content and April 6–7 battle account on 09-048 support 1862. Military locations, opinions, threats and casualty reports are the correspondent’s assertions, not verified editorial statements.

09-048 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 48
09-048-P01
[[lost: left edge]] re not permitted [[obscured]] Camp. On 6th & 7th (Sunday and Monday one week ago) [[obscured]] before this reaches you. There was [[obscured]] splendid battle [[obscured]] Shiloh, (a church house), near Corinth Miss, [[lost: left edge]] our boys done Some [[obscured]] fighting on those days. William went through both days without receiving a Scratch, but, 2 of his Company fell, and Several wounded, one of our near neighbour boys was killed and another wounded, the wounded one came home, I met him on [[inserted: my]] way to Corinth, I was not allowed to proceed, and came back.
The great wonder is that our whole Regiment was not nearly all killed, for they made 7 charges and took a battery every charge. Strange to tell they lost only 25 or 30 men out of their Regiment.
We live about 80 ms from Corinth or Shilo, quite a number of our wounded have come into this region of country. among them one of my Sisters Sons (Shelton) who was Shot through the breast, he is not thought to be dangerously wounded. I had no knowledge of his being in the army untill day before yesterday evening, when I went to Gadsden Station on the M. & oh RR, at which place I understood that he was in that neighbourhood, I went to him Immediately, and Saw him. Charly, he enlisted at or near Nashville. The yankies have possession of Union City (at the crossing of the Mobile & oh & North Western RR, in Obion county) They have Pensacola—You may not be Surprised to hear a Stampede of yankies from Tenn. Price & Van dorn are at Memphis, encamped there with their commands. this has been reported for several days but I have not been Satisfied of the fact untill Since I commenced writing this letter—
You write that Its probable that your boys may come to Tenn, and [[obscured]] may be they are at Memphis with Price. If So, and I learn the fact I will hunt them out, when permitted

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continuation of 09-047. Left edge and stains obscure parts of the text. Battle account is secondhand: the writer explicitly says he was refused permission to proceed to Corinth. Seven charges and casualty counts are his reports, not independently verified figures. “One week ago” is retained despite possible tension with the heading’s date. Charly appears after the reference to his sister’s son Shelton; the syntax associates them but does not provide a complete formal name.

09-049-P01
to visit the encampment—[[obscured]] especially the [[obscured]] generally, dont like yankies [[obscured]] to do with them [[lost: left edge]] as possible, and are as Sullen as a [[obscured]] It has been [[obscured]] circulated for the last few days [[obscured]] Nashville has been recaptured, but I dont Credit the report. All I wish is that It may be true and that every yankey handled without Gloves—
We have a great many men among us, who, I believe would make Splendid tories If they had the Chance, Such men I had rather Shoot than a regularly built Yankey. there are none who dare, at this time to Show their hand, but, If in case the enemy Should get among us we may look out— I have not heard from our friends In Middle Tenn in Some time, the last I heard, they were all well. I [[deleted: suppose]] [[inserted: suppose]] the boys are at Corinth—and If I am ever permitted to visit the encampment I will hunt them out—
I must close, I of late have So much [[lost: left edge]] to writing, It is quite an uphill business for me to Sit down to address a friend, as much as I like to correspond. I will however, answer all the letters written to me from you or any of the friends; Say to them write to us. You will please write on the reception of this—Wife joins me in love to you family and all the Connexion, let them all hear from us—
For the present Farewell
W. W. Nance

09-052 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 52
09-052-P01
Bayou Deglaize La
May the 17th 1864
Dear Father
I embrace the Present Opportunity of writing you A few lines. Although I Dont know how To [[At?]] commence. times are rather exciting At present. we have As you Allridy [[deleted: illegible]] know been fighting nearly every day Since the 12th of April.
We had the hotest time yesterday That we have ever had. the fight commenced in the Morning. heavy Cannonading untill About 1 oclock When we was ordered to charge them in their brest works which we did but was repulsed and had to fall back. losing A great Many killed And wounded. John Morgan was [[lost: bottom edge]]

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continues on 09-053–054. Scan rotated for reading. Bottom edge truncates a line; next page begins “killed,” allowing the sentence’s continuation but not restoring any intervening clipped text. The battle is not assigned a modern name solely from geographic context.

09-053 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 53
09-053-P01
killed. Uncle Alf and gran Jetton was wounded both of them in the leg flesh wounds not dangerous. Also Mr Calaway of our company was wounded. The Sergant Report 12 killed—65 wounded. And 2 Missing. We had [[deleted: illegible]] About 12.000 Men on our Side. But there was not More than half engaged. I dont know the loss of our Side Although it was very heavy. The Yanks had A great Many More Men than we had.
Henry has gone to Texas after Our clothing looking for him back every day I have been in About twenty fights Since I left home and have never received A Scrach yet. Although I have been in Some tight Places Where Minie flew as thick as Hail

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continuation of 09-052. “The Sergant Report” introduces the figures 12 killed, 65 wounded, 2 missing, but the unit covered by that report is not specified. The writer then separately says he does not know his side’s total losses. “Gran Jetton” is retained without expanding the forename. Their leg wounds are reported by the writer as not dangerous.

09-055-P01
[[Swan?]] lake ark
Sept 23rd 64
Dear Father & Mother
Having an opportunity of Sending A letter to Texas I get down beside an old rotten Brush to write you a few lines although I have nothing of interest to write we are camped three miles below the goodloe place on the Arkansas River [[inserted: having fine times]] and no Prospect of A fight. Co D is Detached from the Regt we are camping for Forage [[illegible]] right Smart hard Riding &c I have just Returned from Monticello I was detailed to guard Some cotton Smuglers up there. the health of the command is very good at this time there has been Some chills though not many. As my health is [[illegible]] very good.
Old Cider gave out on the way and I traded him for A Mule Made A very good Swop.
I was glad that Henry got the detail to get clothing But I wish it was I as Mr B M got loss if [[illegible]]
Father you must excuse this Scribbling as I am in a great hurry [[illegible]] But do write to me.
Nothing More at Present, Your Son Bob

EDITORIAL NOTE: Location tentative. “Co D” read as Company D; no regiment number appears in the main letter. Phrase after “Mr B M” remains uncertain and is not expanded. “Cotton Smuglers” is the writer’s description, not a legal finding. The following page contains a postscript and address.

09-057 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 57
09-057-P01
Camp Pisgah La
Oct 15th 1863
Dear Father and Mother
After A long Silence I once more take up my pen to write you A few lines Although I have nothing of Interest to communicate I received your letter to Henry last Monday, and was very glad to hear from home and that you was all well. but was very Sorry to hear of your misfortune. this leaves me in good health I have had A few chills lately but have got clear of them. Henry has gone out with Lieut Cox to [[buy beeves?]] has been gone About two weeks I expect he will return Soon he was in good health when he left.
The health of the command is improving but there is A great deal of Sickness in it yet mostly chills and fever.
Jack [[Levins?]] Jim Lancaster gran Alexander and [[Pickering?]] Started for Texas this Morning on furlough They furlough four from the company every Sixty days my time will come After awhile.
I would have wrote to you Yesterday and sent it by Jack but didnt know that he was going to Start until nearly night. we are looking for old Jef every day with our clothing In hopes he will come Soon as I am getting tired of camp and want to get out on A scout. Wait until after Drill

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continues on 09-058. Purpose of Henry’s trip with Lieutenant Cox is tentative. Two names in the furlough list are uncertain. The parents’ “misfortune” is not explained in this letter.

09-058 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 58
09-058-P01
Drill is over and I resume my pen. we had general review and inspection yesterday morning and Big Drill in the evening with our Regt and capt Pratt Battery the Boys would charge the Battery and they would fire blank cartridges At them it went like A fight sure enough. Col Burford Pitched About like A hog in high rye with [[Hayberg?]] after him—There was A great many Spectators and old Persons tried to show off to an advantage fortunately I was not in the Drill.
Our Regiment drew A fine lot of clothing the other day Henry was lucky enough to get A fine overcoat which he was very much in need of. I drew A pair of Pants and A Shirt we have drawn A Plenty we are living better in the way of eatables at this camp than we ever have Since we have been in the Service. col Burford Says he thinks we will Stay here all winter.
You must excuse this Short letter and bad writing as my pen is very bad Tell Mary to write me and give All the news and Maybe I will answer Nothing More At Present only I Remain Your Obedient Son
R C Orr
P S Gran Jetton and all of your friends are well [[R.C.O.?]]

EDITORIAL NOTE: Conclusion of 09-057. “Persons” is retained as written, possibly referring to Parsons; no silent correction. Name following Burford’s mock-battle antics is uncertain.

Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 59
09-059-P01
Sabine Pass, July 22/62
Sister Lizzy
To day I am able to knock about [[illegible]] though I am still very weak. I recd your letter of 20th this morning you must have forgot to put in a few [[illegible]] by the way you numbered the pages.
It is cloudy and rainy to day the musquitoes are so bad I have to stay in the porch all the time. I am writing on my lap which is all in a [[illegible]]. I recd Fathers and [[illegible]] letters the other day and got Warren to answer them for me as at the time I was not able to write.
If I remember rightly I only said [[illegible: amount or wording at line break]] for a Substitute, this you are all willing to give and more but do not give so much as to impoverish the estate, and render you entirely dependent upon me though I am willing to do all that I can for you in any way, but it might be, after getting one that the time would be extended to [[55?]] and they would take me again and leave you flat. I dont [[illegible]] on a substitute for fear of accident. I know you would like to have me at home and I would like to be at home but at the same time I dont want you to impoverish yourselves for my benefit.
There is no telling the war may soon end or yet it may be a long time first. If it should end soon there might be a large sum of money lost by paying high for a substitute. My advice is not to get one unless you can pay for him without

EDITORIAL NOTE: Letter continues through 09-062, signed George and addressed here to “Sister Lizzy.” The proposed substitute’s price and a possible age limit are too uncertain for a firm historical or financial inference. “Estate” is the writer’s word for property here; it does not establish that his father was deceased. This discusses a proposal, not a completed substitute arrangement.

09-061 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 61
09-061-P01
The entire batt. is prejudiced against him from the manner in which he has treated them, in enforcing the regulations so strictly. He has issued an order for every man in the Batt to have an uniform the men did not like to take them but were forced to. He is out in another order for every man to wear a uniform cap. And there has to be a dress parade every evening. He wont allow the guard to sit down while on guard he has to walk his post continually and not let his gun out of his hands.
Now this looks well enough on paper but it is mighty hard to practice. When the guard is relieved instead of marching direct to the guard house he has to go around with the relief untill all are relieved.
We never done this way before while at Galveston (and we were looking to be attacked every day about the 1st of Jany) when relieved we always went directly to the guard house and went to sleep. While on post we set down lay down and walked as we pleased if we got tired of our gun we would set it down by the side of a house and wrap up in our blanket about two or three times the relief while the Corporal was relieving the first sentinel, would go on ahead and relieve the balance of the Guard before the Corp—could catch up. All this was known to the head officers at Galveston and they never grumbled nary time.

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continuation of 09-059–060. “batt.” expanded as battalion in family reading. The clause beginning “about two or three times the relief” concerns the relief party going ahead of its corporal; it is not a claim that George fell asleep while on post.

09-063 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 63
09-063-P01
Saturday Aug. 8th 1863.
Letter 31
To All at Home.
Writing time has come again but [[illegible]] nothing from home the fault is in the [[illegible]] gap between Beaumont and [[illegible]] every day almost they run off the track or some [[illegible]] they would let us go [[illegible]] any but to waste time.
We have no late intelligence from abroad the [[Pony express?]] came into Beaumont night before last but brought no news. Capt [[Odlum?]] has been absent several days at Beaumont, and returned at night on the [[Dime?]] says he is a little lower in the mouth than any one I have heard express himself yet. Every thing seems to have gone wrong at general headquarters and he has found it out.
This grand scheme of Rio Grand speculation is leaked out and been established fully by circumstantial evidence and there is no longer disguising the facts. Only twenty five bales of Gov. cotton has ever reached Brownsville and no body but Gov. friends have had the control of the transportation. The Mexican breakers were employed by the [[illegible]] of superior officers to take Gov cotton to the Rio and are there yet. It is plain who has made a pile and this is what has disheartened our Capt. It is enough to dishearten any man that has a honest feeling for the Gov.
A man by the name of [[Chisham?]] belonging to our Batt has been wagoning to the Rio grande since we left Galveston he is now with us, says that when [[Magruder?]] was at Brownsville he sent three of his staff to Havanna, yet gave it as his opinion that [[Magruder?]] was acting himself as a private citizen.
Such men have gone to speculating who will [[lost: bottom edge]]

EDITORIAL NOTE: Very faint in places. Continues on 09-064; bottom ending clipped. The cotton quantities, accusation of profiteering, and staff trip to Havana are the writer’s claims or reported speech, not independently verified findings. Two names and the vessel name remain tentative.

09-064 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 64
09-064-P01
I do not know but what I would as soon go to Galveston as to stay here, yet we are not as apt to get as good quarters there again as we did have, but we can see more hear more and have a livelier time generally, if they dont put us to digging dirt and such like [[illegible]]. Some say that Cooks artillery are to take our place, but to make this place defensible it will require both artillery and pickets and plenty of them.
That [[illegible]] how my [[train?]] of ideas is getting shorter than a sheet of paper here lately as I find it difficult to manufacture something without material. To day is my guard day somehow I get my share of the Sunday for guard in this little difficulty of ours. I am to go down the river to night to keep watch in that direction, we have watched in that direction for a long time never to have discovered any thing dangerous. We go after dark and come away before it is light enough to be seen by the enemy.
There is seven prisoners in the guard house now for petty offences, it is quite an easy place so [[illegible]] it and some had rather be in than out there ought to be a lock up for these little petty officers who have not self respect enough to keep themselves out of such places, and put better innocent men by imprisoning them.
Rogers who done the stealing at Dallas and was guarded by us to Houston and there left in charge of the Provost Marshal and there tried and sentenced to work on the fortifications three months was returned the other day to his company for duty, and in about three days was put in the guard house for getting drunk [[illegible]] on guard.

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continuation of 09-063. No signature visible. Faint clauses concerning officers and the final words remain marked. Allegations against Rogers and the reported sentence are attributed to the writer; surname alone does not identify the person beyond this letter.

09-065 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 65
09-065-P01
Sabine City Aug 15th
Letter 32
Sister Lizzie
I received yours of July Monday evening I received yours of July 19th to day and Lauras of Jun 27th. They had all taken a resting spell somewhere on the road I do not know where. Lieut Baily returned from Houston yesterday bringing orders for us to go to Gal. as soon as two companies of Elmores regt one company of [[Goulds?]] regt and [[deleted: illegible]] Capt Jones artillery should come to relieve us, it will be some ten days before we get off if that soon: we are to report to Col De Bray for duty. Lieut Baily says that Sorrells regt are in a state of mutiny and that the troops at Ft Point have turned the cannon on the city, and demand better rations.
It is rather a bad state of affairs if they cant feed men well enough to keep them from mutinying in this confederate gov. but I will learn more about this when I get there. There was a case of insubordination here the other day, Capt [[Odlums?]] Co. or rather the principal part of them refused to drill one morning, giving as a reason for so doing that they had not any soap to wash with and had not had for a long time and that they were out of money and wanted the pay that was due them five months pay is now due. After trying the guard house a few hours they concluded to return to duty.
The spirit of insubordination is abroad and despondency with it, about one half of this Batt. is whipped and ready to give it up as a bad job.
Since Vicksburg has fallen the men look gloomily to the future all communication being cut off with the east, and no reliable cheering news of late

EDITORIAL NOTE: Year not written in the visible heading; context and sequence with Letter 31 support 1863. Continues on 09-066–068. “Gal.” expanded as Galveston. Reports of Sorrell’s regiment and Fort Point are explicitly Lieutenant Baily’s reports. The regiment name before Captain Jones and the captain’s surname remain tentative.

09-068 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 68
09-068-P01
The weather is getting hot down here sure enough, I dont think I ever saw it so hot in Ellis as it is here, there is scarce ever any breeze stirring, hot cloudy and calm. An abundance of watermelons have been brought here from Sabine Bayou in two little lighters and [[schooners?]] which they sell at tolerably fair prices, they are very good as are our water pumpkins can be had tolerably cheap and are pretty good with bread and beef a change, anyhow.
The Zehorlda brought a couple of Co's to relieve us last night. But the order for us to go to Galveston had been previously countermanded so we will stay here for an indefinite length of time yet. I prefer this place to Gal. until the yellow fever season is over, for here we have a chance to skedaddle while at Gal. we would not have. If there is any yellow fever at Houston I have never heard of it I guess it is all a mistake, such reports are apt to get out at this time of year anywhere. I have heard that a great many men are going home from La on short furloughs, but most generally “they have left their certificates of disability behind.” We are all in good health at present, [[Jeems?]] has been complaining for a few days but there is not much the matter with him. I suppose that there is no healthy man here for we are all well so far as I know. Tell [[Essie?]] that I will write to her yet awhile, but I never was born a poet and shall never be as well. I believe I have told all the news
My love to all Your Brother George

EDITORIAL NOTE: Conclusion of 09-065–067, signed George. Vessel name read “Zehorlda,” possibly the same name written elsewhere as “Zehorla”; retained without normalization. Phrase “no healthy man here” is retained as read despite the following statement that all are well. Recipient name in the last request is tentative. Yellow-fever reports and furlough claims are described as things heard, not verified by George.

09-070-P01
Sabine Pass May 14th 63
Number 21,
Sister Lizzie
I received your dates of 29th and 30th ult yesterday, they were mailed May 2 and only eleven days on the road, I dont see why my letters dont reach you, for I have not failed to write weekly.
Since writing before we have had a jolly night, or rather the boys had, for I did not “pitch in.” It seems that the “Staff” are quite fond of rum and they leave no stone unturned to get it, First they took a demijohn from a boat man, next they found a barrel of whisky out in the country, and they took that. Next they took a half barrel of rum from a frenchman. This they reported on their returns as destroyed to keep the soldiers from getting drunk, but they were destroying it by a slow process. At last the boys got tired at the way the “Staff” was doing and determined to finish the whiskey. So one night after tattoo had been beat the cavalry marched up to headquarters and rolled out the whiskey, and called for all hands to come up and drink for it was a free thing. The barrels were carried out in the prairie and every [[inserted: one]] pitched in with cups canteens coffee pots and buckets and near every body got drunk. The staff done all they could to save the whiskey but to no purpose, they could not get a guard in time. C company was only a little behind others that is the cavalry and boat hands. They C were organizing a squad to take the whisky when the others came along. Directly after the [[deleted: boys]] fuss commenced the long roll was beat and Lanier said every man [[lost: left edge]] did not answer to his name had to go in the

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continues on 09-071. A few initial letters at the left edge fade or are clipped, but most words remain secure. “ult” means the preceding month. Tattoo and long roll are military drum signals; no modern clock time is supplied. The incident and the allegations against the staff are George’s account.

Some of the boys came up and told the Capt about it, and asked him if they must fall into line. he told to fall in or not just as they pleased and that none of his men should go in the guardhouse. The federals have been quiet for a good while here, their last freak was to halt our pickets below here who wouldnt halt but kept going when they fired at them but without effect. The lighthouse guard has been discontinued so we have but little to do but cook and eat, the latter we do to perfection. We get a pound and a half of [[deleted: meat]] beef and full rations of meal a day, Every ten days we get about three pounds of sugar a pint of peas a little over half pint of vinegar and [[deleted: to that]] about a pint of molasses sometimes more generally less.
We dont get more than a fourth part as much soap as we need and that very indifferent. I was mistaken about the molasses only a pint to three men for ten days but generally more. Excepting the staples beef and bread you might say we get nothing at all. we have been issued peas twice since we left Galveston and vinegar only occasionally.

09-074 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 74
09-074-P01
Wednesday Evening, July 22
Letter, Number, 28th, 1863
Sister Lizzie,
I have delayed writing longer this time than usual on account of a three days residence at the lighthouse. Col Griffin set a trap to catch some Yankees at the lighthouse. Some body imagined that they saw one or two Yankees there, so last Wednesday night a detachment of 60 or 70 men under Bickley [[invested?]] and took possession of the place without opposition. Warren with a squad of 20 men were left to take in such yankees as might come along. Saturday night they were relieved by Lieut Deen and 20 men, of the latter I was one. We went down as near the L H as we could get in a boat. We got the boat in about thirty feet of the shore, the interval was knee deep mud. One man took a sack of provisions and started ashore he got about half way and stuck fast, Warren and his squad soon arrived with some plank which was laid down to walk on and the rest of us got safe ashore without sticking. Then commenced the battle in real earnest—but not with the mosquitoes instead of Yankees

EDITORIAL NOTE: Reading order of this letter is 09-074, 09-076 (marked Page 2nd), 09-075 (marked page 3rd), 09-077. A possibly superfluous “not” before “with the mosquitoes” is retained as written; sense is clear from the continuation. The opening force appears “60 or 70,” and the two smaller detachments each number 20.

09-075 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 75
09-075-P01
page 3rd
Col Griffin returned yesterday having only gone as far as Beaumont. Some Lieut Col came with him I expect he is the inspecting officer of this district. There is no news of importance in this country, the militia are to be drafted next Saturday. Rumors from the east are still contradictory. Some say that Vicksbg has been taken others say not, though it is pretty generally believed that it has fallen and Port Hudson also. Rosecrans has flanked Bragg back to the Tennessee river, compelled him to abandon his stronghold at Tulahoma.
One report says that Grant and Johnson have had a fight the latter taking 8000 prisoners why did he not do that before Vicks surrendered [[inserted: illegible]] Lee is about to take Pennsylvania, and whip out Hooker in toto, it must all be true I reckon for he never was whipt. It is to be expected that he will clean up the northeast as Grant does the southwest. I wish they would quit their playing and go home, and let every body do the same.
Our prospects of getting away from here are decidedly dull, though we may be called to northern Texas this fall to meet the yankees in that quarter. If Vicksburg has fallen I look for active operations in La this fall, unless they take a notion to work on the other side of the water first.

EDITORIAL NOTE: Read after 09-076, before 09-077. Reports about Vicksburg, Port Hudson, Grant, “Johnson,” Lee, and Hooker are not reconciled or silently corrected to later historical knowledge. The 8,000-prisoner claim is explicitly a report; the remarks about Lee read as skeptical irony. “in toto” means altogether.

09-076-P01
Page 2nd
We fought them manfully until day light when we brought a battery of smoke to bear on them and succeeded to drive them pretty effectually from one room. After waiting & watching for neds last night we came back having caught nothing. No one is there now.
Having arrived in camps, I found our Capt under arrest for refusing to salute Maj Hammer on dress parade, and for giving him a cursing to boot. Maj Hammer is under arrest for drawing a six shooter on Capt Payne. Col Griffin has gone to Houston and Hammer with him. I understand that Hammer is very anxious to resign and go home, he will have opportunities enough after this little affair is cleared up. Capt Odlum now commands this post and Capt [[Mc R?]] the Batt.
Thursday, 23rd
The boat came in late yesterday evening but brought no letter to me, I have not received later dates from home than Lauras of the 24th and 25th of June, what is the reason of this I cannot have any idea for letters have come from Tarrant Co as late as July 6th. Two more deaths have occurred in our Comp, Mark Evans died monday evening and Wm. K. [[Joyn?]] last friday, both were at Beaumont. William [[Joyn?]] had the measles. The sick at this place are doing well,

09-077 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 77
09-077-P01
Well as the steamer leaves this evening I will close. Lieut Col Mc Neil inspected us this morning in grand style, he first reviewed us and then had us to pass in review before him, he then inspected our arms in regular military style, next we had to manœuvre in Batt drill till he got tired of that, and then company drill awhile, then the manual of arms and then we quit, after having been on the parade ground from half past eight until eleven.
So much for so much we were glad to get rid of his presence I assure you, Men like to show their authority “mighty well” in this latitude. Capt Evans has been released from arrest and I think from all that I can learn Major Hammer has been also. Col Griffin assured him so that his resignation would be accepted he has a certificate of disability from the Drs, and this will insure its acceptance. We are glad to get rid of him on any terms, and hope next time we will get a better one.
The Fort is progressing slowly. More darkies have been sent for to work on it when it will be finished it is impossible to say. It is estimated that it will cost the Government $100,000. I wish you would write to me who all were drafted in our county for I have a curiosity to know how many will be or are left.
All hope of a speedy end of the war is abandoned in this part of the country, pretty much everybody believes that Vicksburg has fallen, and the pet notion of foreign intervention has died.
The weather still continues rainy though the last few days have been tolerably pleasant. My paper is about full, so for the present
Goodbye, George

EDITORIAL NOTE: Conclusion of the letter beginning 09-074; reading order 074, 076, 075, 077. Source uses a racial term for the Black people sought for fort construction. Their legal status and whether/how they were compelled are not specified in this passage. Cost is a reported estimate, not an audited expenditure. The name Evans here supplies the captain’s name absent from the arrest statement on 09-076.

09-080 | manuscript

09-080-P01
Number 23
Sabine Pass May 28th 63
As I said I got yours of 7 the other day and now I will answer the more in full. I was sorry to hear that Samm was sick, for sickness is such a disagreeable thing anyhow. I have been quite puny for some time but am about well again. Sabine beef and bread is dog living compared to what I have seen it is true we get a few other articles but no vegetables except what we buy and it has been so dry here this spring that the people made but little more than they have use for, as they live by gardening mostly anyhow they have no farms and all they have to eat is vegetables and beef, besides what they buy. Most of them have large stocks of cattle, but some how this year they failed to make much milk & butter for sale. Some wont sell anything to us but give, all such as these men will go to for anything, others that do sell are soon bought out entirely, and so they have nothing to sell.
It is almost impossible to get washing done at present, the Government dont furnish soap enough to wash socks, and the citizens are out generally. The country for 3 or 4 miles around has been ransacked, to get washing done but the universal cry is “no soap!”
I am very thankful for the socks you sent me, but would much rather had woolen ones. The pills also came to hand by warren and the fine comb, the latter I am happy say I have not needed since I left home and hope I shall not [[lost: bottom line partly cut off in the source image]]

Let me know when the Telegraph will stop and I will try to [[inserted: send]] the news to you for a while as the Tel has doubled its rates your subscription must be nearly out.
A very pleasant shower has fallen this evening the first for about a month, the worst of it was it didnt rain half enough as water is getting scarce in the cisterns.
Sunday May 31st
No boat has yet arrived though the Sunflower is confidently looked for to day. The cause of her long delay lies in the fact that she has been carrying troops to Nibletts bluff for several days past. how many are being sent across I have no idea There must be some danger in that direction of late.

09-083-P01
Galveston Jan [[22th?]] [[1862?]]
Dear Sister
Time passes off in quite a monotonous manner. Galveston is a much prettier place than Houston. there is less mud and the streets can be better drained. The shell for paving purposes are more convenient than at Houston and I think it is a much healthier place. The monotony was somewhat relieved yesterday by the Federals shelling the town and ft point which is about two miles east from here
They commenced about three oclock I reckon and fired 107 shots which did no further damage than the wounding of four men at Ft Point one of whom has since died. A good many of the citizens had returned to their homes these fled to the west of town with their families; some negroes who were at work at the east end of town went through to the west at quick time, some mischevous soldiers threw a barrel head among them and hollered “Theres a bomb” the affrighted blacks fell flat of their faces on the hard pavement.
During most of the engagement I was on top of our quarters in a lookout and [[inserted: could]] see every shot that was fired or rather the smoke from the guns and I could hear the report also.
The most of the firing was done from the Sciota a gunboat whether ironclad or not I do not know it came up in about a mile of what is called the south battery and fired at the town and surrounding country in order I suppose to find out if there was any batteries about, the Brooklyn fired at ft point all the

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continues on 09-084. The heading’s year appears to end in 2, but the reading is uncertain; it has not been silently changed to 1863 to fit the military events described. The day’s suffix also looks irregular. Figures for shots and casualties are the writer’s report. The source’s historical racial wording is retained in the reference transcription.

09-084 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 84
09-084-P01
time and almost every shell after the first few rounds struck its mark.
The Brooklyn shot about four miles and [[deleted: and]] would drop a shell among the tents or in the batteries every time. They shot sufficiently close to cut the [[flagstaff at R R pier?]]. While I was in the lookout a shell from the Sciota came singing its peculiar song directly towards me so Direct it seemed to come that I involuntarily dodged. This was the only one that came near me.
This morning I saw three shells that were fired at us that did not burst, two of them were round and would weigh about 130 pounds the other was an oblong shell fired from a rifle gun it was steel pointed and about five inches thick by fifteen long. There are now five vessels in sight but I do not think they will attack us until reinforcements come up; a flag of truce went out day before yesterday on official business not made public, which learned [[deleted: that]] from the Federals that they intend attacking this place shortly, how much truth and how much bombast there is in this I cannot tell. They say they can whip us here and that they intend doing it but what Mr Yankee intends to do is very uncertain.
All the rigging has been taken off the two barques captured here and is stored away. They cannot get them out for the blockade and the water is too shallow to move them up to Houston and consequently they have to stay here.
They have repaired the Harriet Lane and I understand she is now ready for sea but she cant get out either, steamboats run from here to Houston but little travel is going on.

Sabine Pass Septr 22nd 1864
Dear Brother
I have just recd a bundle of letters from you including sisters & your note from [[illegible: place]] Aug 20.

I am only sorry that so much money tax was not levied sufficient to carry on govt & war & thus depreciated its

09-091 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 91
09-091-P01
dividers & sometimes the protractor also which I think I left at home. A Traverse table is indispensable in making surveys that are irregular in their Shape. I never to be sure did nor understand how to Calculate Latitude & departure which are the base & perpendicular of a triangle of which the distance is the hypothenuse and degree for angle of departure known. In practice the degree being known either line of the triangle may be measured & the table gives the other two. All irregularities in surveys can & must be reduced to triangles in calculating area The base & perpendicular multiplied together & product divided by 2 gives the area.
In practice where you hold a survey upon another you consider the lines of the first as the base & in diverging from their direction you consider the divergence the departure & the last lines your latitude irrespectively of the cardinal points. Field notes must balance the traverse table is the simplest & easiest means of [[rectifying?]] or determining the length of unknown lines in irregular surveys.
In practice the measurements seldom close either less than a chain or two where the ground is [[uneven?]]. You consequently [[choose?]] the most favorable side of a survey & leave it so long to be run measured. For the same reason in so work establish your beginning corner until you run all round & then establish it where

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continuation of 09-090, ending mid-sentence before 09-092. Some phrasing is irregular as written, including “I never to be sure did nor understand” and “in so work establish.” The family reading explains the evident caution about fixing a starting corner but does not present this historical letter as a modern surveying manual. “Latitude” and “departure” are technical surveying terms, not ordinary geographic latitude and a journey’s departure.

Surveys not to one should as nearly as possible be square—fractions of less than 80 acres not to be left between surveys. [[Avoiding?]] [[illegible]] boundaries unless it be entirely Surrounded vacant. When it is necessary to have a [[line?]] of a new Survey upon an old one it is desirable to point the corners or line trees in a new direction. You must then in your field notes adhere to the direction first taken. For instance if you begin on a line running N.60°E. you may trace that N but you must turn E S & W & North to the boundary line & then close down by that; & in this line in order to come as near to a square as possible [[deleted: your]] the mean between your N. & S lines should equal your E. or W. lines.
In practice it is best always to adapt the variation of the needle first to correspond to the old lines. 10° is the most common but they vary from 9° to 12° & sometimes even more. It is the custom lately to state at the bottom of field notes the var. used.

09-101 | manuscript

09-101-P01
Houston March 19th/65
Sister Lizzie
Again I will write you from this place with but little idea how long we will be permitted to remain. Nothing have we heard yet in a reliable shape connected with our future movements though tis the general opinion that we will go east of the Miss sometime this Spring. But very few have any inclination to travel in that direction I assure you, though if ordered twill be very few who will refuse to go. I have heard no late news of any importance lately. A few days ago a rumor was afloat that a battle had occurred between Sherman & Beauregard in which the former was routed and the latter killed. The papers however say nothing about it. Last authentic accounts from there said Sherman and Hardee were racing for Charlotte and Sherman was about to get there first.
Evidently there will be active times there this spring and if some Yankees dont come this way Somebody from this Dept will have to go East of the Mississippi sure. One of two things is evident. Either an attack is feared at Galveston or the troops on the Coast are to be relieved and sent to the field. All the old troops from La & Ark are coming this way

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continues on 09-102. March 19, 1865 is written in the heading. Reports of troop movements and the supposed death of Beauregard are the writer’s contemporary information; he explicitly says the newspapers do not confirm the rumor. “Miss” expands to Mississippi in the family reading.

09-102 | manuscript

09-102-P01
I got a letter from Henry Orr dated 13th inst in which he [[deleted: said]] said he expected they would move to the Brazos Country in a few days as the forage was exhausted about Waverly, and said for me to answer him at Hempstead. De Brays Regt is at Hempstead now. Tom wrote from Tyler under date 10th and says his old Regt is on the march for Hempstead. Walkers old Division is ordered I understand also [[deleted: the]] Greens old Brigade. This I think is indicative of apprehensions of an attack on the coast or Starvation in La & Ark.
We still have good health and live pretty well all things considered. We joined funds the other day and bought a Sack of flour & thirty pounds of Coffee. So we have Coffee & Biscuit at our house. This makes about 45 pound Coffee which we have bought since we came here. Confed money has fallen to 27 again and not very current. Specie is also Scarcer than it was, goods generally a lower owing to the Scarcity of money. Blockade Running Still continues at Galveston by which means goods plentiful in the Market. Cotton Cards brought 1.60 per pair by the dozen pair at auction. Today I went to hear the old presbyterian, had an excellent Discourse in which no allusion was made to the present War any way, the Confed, Jeff, [[deleted: Abe]] Abe or any other political Dignitary.
As ever your brother Geo.

EDITORIAL NOTE: Conclusion of 09-101. “27” is recorded without a stated conversion basis; it should not be presented as a verified exchange rate to a specific currency. “Cotton Cards” are tools for preparing cotton fiber, not playing cards. Initial deletion before the repeated Abe is retained.

March [[22nd?]]
Sister Lizzie
I will answer yours which came in Jodys, date 4th No 7. Received day before yesterday.
I can say that you are improving a good deal in letter writing and a few more severe criticisms would do you some good, but I dont intend to be hard on you. Merely Correct a few words occasionally Such as “[[horrizon?]]” “[[pos ble?]]”
To day is a very pleasant one. The sea breeze blows all the time now that winter has broke and spring come. If it was not for the warm atmosphere I could not tell that spring had opened, for roses have bloomed all winter and the numerous evergreens never change their appearance. The gardens look well as they have done all winter. There is no timber on the Isle

09-108 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 108
09-108-P01
To all at Home. Houston Texas March 10th/65
It was with the deepest Sorrow that I heard of the death of my Sister through Capt Evans who came down a few days ago. Little did I expect to hear of so sad an event, it came unexpectedly but ah! too true, and we can but weep over the departed with unavailing Sorrow, for they cannot be recalled, but the evidences of the Higher Hope of immortality which they have left, gives comfort to the sorrowing hearts that are left behind.
To me it is a greater Source of happiness to know that She died in [[full?]] hope of Heaven and everlasting bliss, than to have been crowned [[the?]] richest Queen of the Earth. and while we mourn her loss [[illegible: fold obscures part of line]] her gain. It looks hard for her to be called [[away?]] from her young family, but the ways of Providence are [[always?]] the best and tis but meet that we yield without a murmur to its decrees. Sad indeed it is to the children to be thus early deprived of their protector, deprived of her care and love [[such?]] as only a mother can bestow and thrown almost upon the World for awhile. Sympathy for them increases our sorrow for [[our?]] loss, but we must do all that lies in our power in their [[behalf?]], Seperated by fate or fortune from their only parent.
More than ever I feel that I am needed at home but less [[and?]] less the Chances appear to me for returning any time shortly, the future grows darker and darker as we advance and [[not one?]] ray of light appears ahead.

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continues on 09-109, signed Geo. Douglas. The deceased sister is not named on these two pages. Dark folds and a clipped left edge obscure several words; bracketed reconstructions are not certain readings. The phrase about the children’s “only parent” is preserved without inferring the other parent’s fate.

09-109 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 109
09-109-P01
Rumors are plentiful about being ordered across the Miss river and to La and I am pretty confident that that we will start Somewhere east by the first of next month. We may be sent east of the river and if so the Chances for a single individual to remain on this side are very Slim, for under Such circumstances no transfers would be given. The men are almost unanimously opposed to such a move but you all know what orders are. It is reported that Lee has ordered 30,000 troops east of the Miss and if this be true I look for the worst. However I will not trouble myself about it any more than I can help, only wish my term of service was out.
No news reaches us except what comes through the blockade. Sherman is occupying the coast cities almost [[without?]] opposition and [[Lee?]] is concentrating. Indicating I think a field Campaign this year almost altogether; Perhaps twill hasten the war to a close, by subjugation if no other way, any way almost would suit me now.
To day has been fast day and all has been quiet. I do not attend their war meetings and preachings.
The Country is ready to receive anything in the Shape of Govt now, will submit to anything, their Spirit is broken. It is late and cold so I will close.
With best love to all I remain as ever affectionately
Geo. Douglas.

EDITORIAL NOTE: Conclusion of 09-108, dated March 10, 1865. “Lee” and “without” are obscured by a dark fold. The asserted troop order is explicitly a report, and the statements about the country’s spirit are the writer’s opinions. “Fast day” refers to a day of fasting, not speed.
