09-111 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 111
09-111-P01
Sabine Pass, March 11th/64 — No 60
Sister Laura
This weeks mail brought me your letter of the 21st ult, and found us all on the Square. I see you have had some cold weather as [[inserted: well]] as us, from what I have been able to learn the past winter has been tolerably severe in every place.
The weather still continues very dry and unless we have rain soon all the cistern water will be gone, and the well water is quite indifferent. In and around the precinct of Sabine Pass everything moves on in the usual way, but little arises to excite attention, and the general pleasantness of the weather tends to increase that disease commonly known as laziness, and which always prevails in a garrison to a considerable extent. There is two of our Co sick at this time, one at Beaumont and one here; both pneumonia one caused by the measles the other an ordinary attack, neither from what I can learn very dangerous.
The Clifton has not yet departed, made an unsuccessful attempt to go about two weeks ago, grounded on an oyster reef at high tide and lay out of plum a day and night which sprung a leak somewhere in the bottom though not bad enough to keep her in port, she will try again the first favorable time.

EDITORIAL NOTE: Letter No. 60. Continues on 09-112–114. “Ult” means the preceding month. “Out of plum” is retained as written; the family reading interprets it as lying out of upright alignment. Medical descriptions are the writer’s report, not a modern diagnosis.
====================================================================
09-112 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 112
09-112-P01
Our foreign news is quite meagre, merely what we get from the papers and of course we get the best side of the tale if it is not always to be relied on. Lying has got to be so fashionable that almost every source of intelligence is filled with it, somebody, or some people rather are getting so well up to, and used to it, that they can lie without knowing it, it seems. Twice has Sherman been badly whipt in Miss! The first time he ran pretty fast no doubt, but unfortunately for the South the Rebs walked in the lead. If his last Skedaddling was like the first, where now is Polk? The farther a tale travels the bigger it gets, this rule works everywhere and now Since the fall of Vicksburg tales have to come a roundabout way, consequently they assume large proportions. No reliance can now be placed in the details of affairs east of the Miss, only the general items can be credited and the general features of the case are rather dark.
Some Strange ideas have worked themselves into the upper country, I see by the tone of your letters. Yanks and Rebs are on better terms Westward than here if they allow Schooners to run in and out at will, only fire a few blanks at them, here they always Shoot to hurt. When no better amusement presents itself the Yankees Shell our Pickets on the beach.

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continuation of 09-111. “Foreign news” here is the writer’s label for news beyond his immediate area, including east of the Mississippi. His claim that Sherman was twice defeated is ironic: the following sentences question the reports. The family reading keeps that irony explicit.

09-113 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 113
09-113-P01
Several came ashore the other evening about dark but the cavalry failed to take them in, couldnt find them in the night. Evidently the people of your section are badly whipt, even worse than the Soldiers, or express themselves more freely. Maybe we are bold and maybe not, who knows.
Fewer remarks are made about military affairs now than formerly, all somehow seem to be careless about it any way. To brag about Confederates and run down Yankees is an old song worn out long ago, and tis scarcely ever hummed nowadays. No one pretends to say how the Women and children will live after the supply now on hand is gone nor do they seem to take any lively interest about it. However the present stillness may not last beyond a few weeks, and then, all may be storm and commotion again.
And still they marry! I was Surprised to hear of Mary [[Pattons?]] union for I Supposed She was too young to leave her mamma. Em Chapman I only know by character and hardly by that. She is cousin to Lizzie I believe, wonder if Lizzie will do likewise. White folks are very uncertain, so are the Women. Dont marry yourself off to Some gentleman of the “Bush” merely because you get a chance, better call back “[[Bowle?]]” first, though he is aged, and rather “red” headed,

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continuation of 09-111–112. Mary’s surname and the quoted nickname at the end remain uncertain. The statement that Em Chapman is Lizzie’s cousin is qualified by “I believe” in the source. “Gentleman of the Bush” is left as the writer’s phrase, without identifying a particular man.

09-114 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 114
09-114-P01
A raid of Jayhawkers towards Nibletts from some of the La Swamps has excited some little attention. I understand Greens Brigade has been ordered to that region for their benefit. There is quite a a nest of them beyond Calcasieu lake from here and have been doing some mischief in that region. It is reported that they are sustained by Banks, but every species of rascality now days is attributed to Yankee credit.
I have a sufficiency of paper to last Six months so you need not trouble yourselves on my account. I am very much obliged to Sister for her present, but will not need it for some time to come. In the varying scenes of war I hope I may have a chance to be at home and get [[inserted: it]] by the time I have use for it. Tell her I will try to write to her during this month. I received Marys letter the other day, and will have to send her word that She is Still very modest; She had better outgrow that.
One of our co has been released from the guard house; Gilbert the man that left [[Millican?]] sick and went home last fall.
We still get plenty to eat such as it is, but the quality is rather poor. Some of the troops on Galveston Island have not had beef for a week. The last the got was so poor they buried it with the honors of War, and have refused to take any more because it was no better.
Affectionately, George

EDITORIAL NOTE: Conclusion of the March 11, 1864 letter, 09-111–114. Banks’s supposed support of Jayhawkers is explicitly reported hearsay; George questions the tendency to blame every offense on Yankees. The place/name after “left” is uncertain. The present from “Sister” is not identified beyond the surrounding discussion of paper.

09-115 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 115
09-115-P01
Sister Laura Houston April 11th 1865
I promised last week to write a larger letter this week so I suppose I will have to comply with Said promise. Wednesday morning I Started for Velasco, twas dry though cloudy, arrived at Columbia on the Brazos River at four oclock in the evening. Columbia is a Small place noted only for being the terminus of the [[H.T. & B.R.R.?]] The Country traversed by this road is low and flat, mostly prairie and very fertile. Tis thinly Settled, though a few rich planters live along the route. The Brazos is the prettiest river that I have Seen in this latitude, tis about one hundred yards wide and very deep, the banks are lined with Cottonwood and willow, and covered with quick Sand.
Left Columbia thursday morning on the Steamboat “Era No. 3” for Velasco distant about fifty miles by the river route. The weather still continued cloudy wind blowing [[lost: start of line]] and from the east. Eight miles below Columbia is Brazoria [[also?]] a Small place on the river bank in the woods. This [[is?]] the only town below Columbia. The boat Stopped [[frequently?]] along to take in men belonging to Bates Regt [[who?]] had been in the bottoms hunting and cutting poles to [[build?]] cook houses with at the mouth of the river.
[[lost: fragments of another line at bottom edge]]

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continues on 09-116–118. Left edge and bottom of the reproduction clip parts of words and a following line. The railroad initials are tentative and have not been silently expanded. The boat name reads Era No. 3. This is the writer’s travel description; distances and assessments of settlement are his own.

09-116 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 116
09-116-P01
Some four or five miles above Velasco the timber [[deleted: gave]] [[inserted: gives]] out and the river emerges into the open prairie. Like Sabine the Country is low and flat, the banks of the river Scarcely eighteen inches high. Near the lower edge of the timber was Some of Magruders ground hoggery in the Shape of a Small field fortification with two embrasures for guns. About two miles above the mouth is another earthwork mounting one gun. Arrived at Velasco at near three oclock, wind very hard from east and pretty cold, hunted up Hd Qrs [[G.C.M.?]] & turned over my prisoner according to orders and then began looking about for Dock. I Soon met with him but would not have known him, His beard has not heard of a razor for years and besides he is tolerably gray as much so as father. He was in good health but very sick of the war and anxious to hear from home as he had not heard Since the battle of Shiloh.
Velasco is on the east Side of the river and Quintana on the west. The principal portion of the troops are at Quintana Hd Qrs are at Quintana. Velasco Contains five or Six dwellings only, Quintana about twice that No. The two Cities are exactly opposite each other, the river between is about three hundred yards wide. There is no bay at the mouth. There is a fort on each side immediately on the beach, each commanding the Channel

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continuation of 09-115. “Dock” is not expanded to a formal name. The headquarters abbreviation is tentative. “Ground hoggery” is the writer’s mocking description of Magruder’s earthworks. The remark about Dock’s gray beard provides no age or exact relationship.

09-118 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 118
09-118-P01
There was no life boat nearer than the wreck of the Acacia ten miles off on the beach to windward, and no boat could be launched on the open Sea in [[deleted: illegible]] Such a gale. Up to the time the boat left nothing had been done for the relief [[deleted: of]] of the poor fellows who were left clinging in the ropes and nothing could be done without a life boat and that was not obtainable. I never Saw so rough a Sea in my life before and hope never to see again when a vessel is in distress. There was no Chance to get the men off untill the Sea calmed. Saturday morning the wind was from the north and if they had not fallen from the rigging from exhaustion they were doubtless relieved. But two nights and a day was a long time to hang on to ropes and the Vessel rocking like a cradle in the Sand with every Swell of the Sea, and threatning to part.
Friday I returned to Columbia, it rained a good portion the day and was disagreeably cold it continued raining friday night & Saturday, Saturday I came on to Houston, arrived in the night and found the mud very deep & thin. Everything had been in an uproar on account of Whartons death but all was [[deleted: illegible]] quiet.
[[separate block: inverted writing above main text]]
All well here at present. We are not ordered away yet tis rumored that transportation has been ordered for 30,000 men — George [[Dou... ?]]

EDITORIAL NOTE: Conclusion of 09-115–117, April 11, 1865. Inverted closing read separately after rotation. The final surname is clipped. George says the men were “doubtless relieved” only if they had survived until the sea calmed; this is his supposition, not a witnessed rescue. “Acacia” is the reading of the earlier wreck’s name.

The defeat of Sibley at new Iberia is confirmed by report but as yet I have seen no published acct of it. It is said that he lost 250 killed, and is now himself under arrest for being drunk on the day of the fight.

09-121 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 121
09-121-P01
Sister Lizzie. Galveston May 4th 1865
Since I last wrote you we have changed base to this city. We came down yesterday on a Special train, quitted our old quarters after breakfast and got into our new ones time enough to get Supper. The weather was fine and altogether twas the most pleasant move we ever made. On the Second we were reviewed by Col Spaight, marched about over the principal part of Houston in column of platoons, owing to the absence of O Briens Co our position was on the left wing of the regt (“the tail” as tis called) and had to pad along behind a Co of Creoles who could neither keep a line or time or distance. In Consequence we Showed only at a moderate advantage. Several of the Ladies were out to to See us though no excitement at all was displayed. Scarcely ever a kerchief waved and “never a yell.” One little “[[Husky?]]” in her teens looked So much like She wanted to do Something I lifted my hat to her and She acknowledged the Same by a polite bow, I did not excite further notice afterwards.
Many were the regrets [[deleted: that]] of the Citizens at our departure, Some of the most prominent did their best to persuade Magruder to let us remain but he would not hear to them. They (the citizens) gave the regt a box of Tobacco and 620 pounds of Coffee on the morning of our leaving, and Some Said they would be willing to pay “C” Co $10.00 per month Specie per man to let us Stay. That Shows how we Stand in Houston after a residence of five months. Our being moved is explained in few words. Magruder wants Ashbel Smith to command Galveston island [[El... ?]]

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continues on 09-122. Final line is partly clipped. The word George places in quotation marks for a teenage onlooker is uncertain and is not replaced by a more familiar epithet. His description of the other company and local opinion is retained as his perspective. “Specie” means coin.

on the island but Elmore was Senior Col to Smith and must be removed and Spaight was the only junior Col in the Sub district to Smith, so we came for Smiths accommodation.

09-123 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 123
09-123-P01
Sister Lizzie, Galveston Texas May 7th 1865
Yours of 22d ult came to hand last evening, one must evidently be lost as there Seems to be a lack of connection. As to what I promised to tell you when I got back from Velasco I can Say I believe I forgot it, however twas only Jody going home which was then only prospective. The Capt says tell Jody to not hurry back, get what he went for if possible, no one has come in Consequently cant give an extension of time, Jody will not be looked for before the 1st of June nohow and not a great deal then unless transportation can be had conveniently.
Galveston is badly Shattered by hard treatment, marks of abuse are everywhere visible, tis not near as pretty a city as it was two years ago, though tis ahead of Houston yet in beauty. Business has Stagnated, nothing is doing, the city looks deserted. Most of the wealthier Classes have gone, the poor are still here but there is no employment for them and how the get along is more than I can tell, no money in circulation that I have yet observed, all the business is done at Houston and Galveston is neglected and forgotten.
There are Several regts here I do not know how many. They are quartered in every part of the city, and everywhere They have been they have Succeeded in ruining the houses. The Tremont house and Island City hotel are worthless. Every fence and old house has been burned for wood that any pretext could be found to commence on. Magruder has ditched and dug this end of the island full of holes thus ruining the landscape. An unbroken breastwork extends from the South Battery to Ft [[Scurry?]] and I dont know how much further. All the Sand hills between the S Battery and Ft S. have been leveled by order of Bankhead Lt Col, but under the influence of the wind they are rapidly reforming. [[illegible: clipped final line, includes “Street back near the Court house”]]

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continues on 09-124. The reference to the fort is tentative; the final line is clipped. The captain’s message about Jody is not a surviving formal extension of leave. Descriptions of poverty, housing damage and military earthworks are the writer’s observations and judgments.

Well now for News! Great and multiform are the rumors afloat but from them all this much can be deduced without peeping behind the Scenes. Johnston has either Surrendered or in Such a fair way too that he cant avoid it, but of the details you can [[know?]] as much as I. Now for behind the curtain. It has been rumored for Sometime that there was Some unpublished news on hand in fact this was definitely known, Flake of the Bulletin said as much. Of this news I have got an inkling. Col Wilkes has just arrived from New O. paroled, and Says Sherman and Johnston have come to the agreement that Johnston Surrender the Confederate Army everywhere, turn over all the arms [[deleted: illegible]] to the several State arsenals, disband the troops and Send them home. The Several State governments to continue in their present organizations, only renounce the Confed and renew their allegiance to the U.S. local laws and officers to continue as they are and all return to the Union. And an armistice of forty days agreed on to consult the Washington Cabinet. The Cabinet rejected the propositions as they recognized State Govts. Grant says he will sustain Shermans course with his army as it is a Military Surrender; made with the approval of Breckenridge and Davis. So matters stand if my inkling is correct.
Warren is my informant and he is not likely to jump at a conclusion of this kind, he thinks the war over and that this news is only Suppressed untill it come officially for this Dept to give up and go home, and let the Change be effected as quietly as possible. If this is not premature a couple of months will wind up the Drama. Very likely a good deal of it is ahead of the hounds, yet the air of mystery around the published accounts warrant some surmises.
Stoneman has made a raid in rear of Johnson and destroyed an immense amount of Supplies, Railroads and R.R. bridges, this is unpublished news, came by Wilkes. The foregoing you can take for what tis worth I cant vouch [[for its correctness?]] [[lost: rest of final line]]

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continuation of 09-123. No clear signature survives at the clipped bottom. This is a chain of reported information through Wilkes and Warren, expressly qualified by George. The described terms and claimed forty-day armistice have not been presented as verified historical facts. Johnston/Johnson spellings are retained as they occur.

09-125-P01
Sister Lizzie Houston Feby 26th 1865
Your last of 11th inst came to hand a day or two ago. Glad to hear that you were well of the Sore eyes [[for?]] the little experience which I have had with them has abundantly proved to me that they are unpleasant in the highest degree, fortunately however I have been but very little bothered with them so far.
The past week has been very fair and very foul, Some days it rained and [[some?]] it never though all in all quite a quantity has [[fallen?]] during the past week. Friday and friday night it rained [[very?]] hard. Though Saturday was a pretty day and to day the [[mud?]] has dried very fast. Spring has opened I think [[in?]] this latitude, Some few cold days will come yet but [[none?]] to do any harm I predict.
Prices current this [[week?]] a little higher than last. Confederate Money has [[risen?]] to 25, and not a great deal in circulation. There Seems to be a determination to reduce the circulation [[of?]] it Somehow though Something extraordinary will be [[accomplished?]] if it ever becomes good again, and I think [[nothing?]] will ever make it good but an uncompromising [[tyranny?]] carried on under the immediate Supervision of [[the?]] Military, and plenty of that will be Served up during [[the?]] ensuing year in all kinds of Style to Suit Vendors,

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continues on 09-126–128. The supplied reproduction clips many line beginnings; reconstructed words are bracketed. The currency figure “25” has no explicit exchange basis. No modern medical diagnosis is assigned to “Sore eyes.”

09-126 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 126
09-126-P01
War news this week is very meagre. No fighting going on which has amounted to anything of importance reported, Since peace prospects were broken off. But very little truth ever escapes these latter days I opine owing to the precarious condition of Confed affairs east of the Mississippi. There is a good deal of “Freedom of Conscience” and “Speech” and “Press” I presume [[under?]] the present regime of Military [[Despotism?]], I presume [[it?]] is under and a long ways under, So far under that it will never get out. “So mote it be.” There is always a way to patch up broken places and tis really amusing to see the manner in which States rights are patched, & all other Strongholds [[of?]] Liberty. All are justified under the plea of “Military Necessity” and he is not a “patriot” who growls at anything done by the Government when the ultimate object is Laudable.
All means are expedient just and proper and even Laudable [[when?]] one iota of good can be accomplished. It is nothing [[more?]] than the part of a “Good Patriot” to Surrender all he [[has?]] in property produce and Personal Liberty to the Govt [[for?]] “the time being” to accomplish the “Glorious End” of “[[Southern?]] Independence.” It is better to Sacrifice the “Last [[woman?]] & Child” on the “Altar of Liberty” than to Submit [[to?]] Yankee rule! Anihilation is preferable to “Such Slavery.” [[And?]] he is a coward and a knave who will not do all for his [[country?]]. Such is the Spirit of the Fire Eating press of to day

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continuation of 09-125. The left edge clips several words. This passage is sustained sarcasm criticizing the “Fire Eating press”; the extreme demands are not George’s recommendations. Tentative “Despotism” is partly overwritten. Quotation marks in the source are retained.

09-127 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 127
09-127-P01
Brave Editors behind desks, and brave legislators in Congress brave old men in chimney corners Smoking pipes and brave boys under the Conscript age can talk about what “Well do” with the Yankees how long “Well fight” and all this Sort of thing. Men who never smelled burnt powder and never will, will fight longer than any body else, and those who talks most of fighting are the very ones that never do any of it. Some of the Stump Speaking, fire eating, patriots, who at the beginning of this war Said that they would Spill the “last drop of blood” told an unconscious truth, they will be the last to Spill a drop of “blood.”
I went to the M. E. Church to day, house was full of Soldiers Citizens and Ladies. There Seems to me to be more ugly Women in this City than any place I was ever at. As long as I have been here I do not remember of having Seen a handsome one yet. They always Spoil their looks with Superfluous clothing Some fancy touch Somewhere or everywhere reveals a [[soft?]] place in the “Phrenological Regions.” There is [[too?]] much of the Spirit of Novelty among them to Suit me, [[Vanity?]] in other words, a morbid desire to display Something [[new?]] that will attract attention, reminding of Burns
“O wad Some power the giftie gie us”
“To See oursels as ithers See us”
“’Twad from many a blunder free us, An foolish notion”

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continuation of 09-125–126. Left edge clips a few words in the lower passage. The disparaging statements about women are preserved as the writer’s opinion. His quotation attributed to Burns is transcribed in the wording visible here, not corrected from an outside edition. “M. E.” is expanded as Methodist Episcopal in the family reading.

09-128 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 128
09-128-P01
6h P.M. This Evening I took a Stroll through the western part of the city which presented quite an interesting picture when compared with the business portion. Everything was quiet and in Sunday attire. Some were Strolling the Streets enjoying the balmy Spring air and pleasant Sunshine but by far the greater portion were grouped in their handsome parlors passing the time, apparently, pleasantly enough.
Pleasant Cottages and their homelike associations are pleasant to look at even if they cannot be [[deleted: illegible]] enjoyed at the present by me. Groups of merry children playing on sunny slopes and in grassy yards reminded me of days past but fondly recollected. Scenes which cannot recur but can always be held freshly in the Memory when types of them are presented to the view, and nothing can bring back to mind the Scenes of the past as quick as groups of gay children.
The Church bell is ringing and I will attend So will close this and mail as it will go up tomorrow. I do not remember Miss Luna or Kate [[Denny?]] but Miss Lizzie K. I do. Tell the girls to “go it while they are young” for when they get old may be they Cant. With Best love to all I am as ever your Brother George

EDITORIAL NOTE: Conclusion of 09-125–128, February 26, 1865. The surname after Kate is tentative. “Gay” has its period sense of cheerful. No childhood location is identified in this recollection.

09-129 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 129
09-129-P01
Sister Lizzie Houston Dec 11th 1864
Your letter of 19th ult has been Recd. Found all present well in body and mind So far as I am capable of judging. During the past week we have had plenty of cool and Some cold weather. Sufficient I think unless the weather turns [[illegible: fold]] again to clear the city of yellow fever. There has been a good deal of it here lately but confined exclusively to citizens houses. No cases have occurred among those who have returned Since the freeze of 20th Nov except Such as occupied houses where it had been during the Summer. I feel no apprehensions of it breaking out among the troops as we are quartered in houses where none has been this Season.
I attended church this morning at the Methodist Church, Speaker and Sermon were neither extra and congregation Small for a city. Up in one corner was an Organ from which music was pumped for the occasion. A big Negro worked the handle, while a Lady fingered the keys Scientifically.

EDITORIAL NOTE: Letter continues through 09-134. Dark fold obscures words about a change in the weather. George’s belief that cold weather and prior house occupancy governed yellow fever risk is recorded as a historical belief, not a medical explanation. The organ attendant’s race is stated; his name and legal status are not.

09-130 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 130
09-130-P01
Music is as much out of place in church as a dog in a parlor, I felt like I was at preaching untill the the organ began [[moaning?]] then I felt as though I was at a party. I dont See where people get the doctrine of Music in churches, tis not in the Testament as I can find, if it is it is in Some unnoticed corner where my perceptions has never reached.
Last Sunday I went to hear the Episcopal. They have quite a large brick church built on the Catholic plan of Gothic Architecture Superb and magnificent. The Parson came out of a closet in one corner with a robe on Catholic fashion, knelt by a desk a moment in Secret prayer where every body could See him; then began the Service. The Worship is read part by the preacher and members, he reading one verse aloud and all of them the next, in prayer he repeats a sentence and then the members all repeat it audibly after him. They Sing Psalms in stead of hymns which Sounded Very well, being diversified a little in the tune yet in perfect harmony. After Service followed the Catechism of the youthful members to See what progress they were making towards full membership; the repeating of the Creed &c, the Creed is identical with that of the presbyterians. [[illegible: words obscured by fold]] very good if they follow what they preach.
Each Child is baptized in infancy, and two persons Standing by act as “Sponsors” Pledging themselves, in case the childs parents die or any other accidents happen that will render them incapable of taking care of the child, to take and raise or See that the child is raised in a proper and religious Manner. There is a great deal of form and Ceremony about their Worship resembling the Catholics a good deal. Preaching is tolerably plain, but there is so much fashion and Show about it that I dont much like it.
I am pretty much the Same opinion as “Fanny Fern” on these matters; “True religion may go to Church in yellow gloves

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continuation of 09-129, followed by 09-131. Two columns read left then right. The fold interrupts the sentence about the creed. Accounts of denominational practice are the writer’s understanding, not editorially verified doctrine. A quotation he attributes to Fanny Fern begins at the bottom and continues on the next scan.

and embroidered handkerchiefs, worth five hundred dollars but I dont believe it!” Though I do not know as I have any right to so judge the people of Houston because they are wealthy.
I have noticed Several new Style Ladies Hats on the Street. The Kind I like best is high crowned narrow brimmed leghorn hats which does Some better I think than the old fashioned broad brims that used to [[deleted: illegible]] about So Conspicuously on the prairies. In my humble opinion however the old fashioned close Split bonnetts [[deleted: illegible]] the handsomest articles that ever a woman wore on her head. You may call that old fashioned and out of date in this day of Splash and dash when brilliants are all the [[rage?]], but it is modest, and that is the nicest quality which ever adorned a woman no matter what the world and the balance of mankind may Say to the contrary. above all things be modest.

09-132 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 132
09-132-P01
Sunday night 11th — 7 Oclock. By candle light I resume to give a few more ideas in my usual disconnected Style of composition and flit. The boys are going to preaching to the Methodist Church So I will be alone, too cold for me to go without they would let music alone and have preaching instead of fun.
There are auctions almost every day in town, dry goods of almost every description at very high prices though coming down a little, the figures are a little under what I wrote last. Flour is plenty in town by the wholesale or retail in lots to Suit purchasers. When asked where it all comes from the answer is invariably “Up the Country.” I have not heard of a great deal being Sold in that Country to Citizens, thought the Govt took all for the army &c &c.
The latest news is Some little Stirring. Sherman has made a bold move into Ga much to the astonishment of all thereby creating a great Stir in military Circles. For once he outgeneralled Hood and all his advisers, [[lost: final words clipped]]

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continuation of the December 11, 1864 letter. Bottom of the source reproduction clips the last line. The writer contrasts flour for sale with his impression that the government had requisitioned it. This is not evidence of a specific theft or diversion.

09-133 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 133
09-133-P01
It is a mistake about Magruder being ordered back to Texas. It is Strange how men who ought to know Start and credit Such reports. Walker will still continue to Command here and furloughs will continue to jog along as usual. Spaight is doing his best to get all details ordered in, if all were present the Regt would number nearly one thousand. This is now about the largest Regt in the State.
There is Somewhere in the neighborhood of a dozen home on leave from this Co now. Only one has thought enough of the fair to marry so far. If accounts be true Eddings, and old “bach” married a widow in [[Stewart?]] a few days ago, he has not yet returned to Camps.
You were a little mistaken on Shialot on the war question, Soldiers generally profess more patriotism than they actually feel for they dont know what Kind of people they are dealing with, and always make sure to be on the Safe Side whether they are or not.
On the Subject of Matrimony I confess I was no little astonished, though I am in the habit of doing things by fits and starts, but this Start Stumped me. I was not aware that She had ever done any thing disreputable. True I learned Henry had denounced his intentions but I thought this was merely a lovers or Something of that Sort. What else I learned merely Settled an opinion I long ago had formed, Viz; Lack of moral Courage and Self resolution. I positively know now nothing more than I knew three years ago, of what may or may not have happened Since I left home or even in the Service rather, I am totally ignorant; nor can I Say I care to know. So here the Subject must drop. [[He?]] had better let marrying alone and go to Mexico and get out of troublous times. The negro is bound to be freed before this war ends, and Jeff Wont give it up as long as he can get a white man or negro to fight for him. “Mr Southern is Some by himself.”

EDITORIAL NOTE: Continuation of 09-132. “Shialot” is the literal place/name reading; no identification is certain. Location of Eddings’s marriage and a pronoun near the bottom are tentative. The private discussion does not name the woman and George expressly disclaims knowledge; no allegation is treated as established fact. His expectation of emancipation is a prediction written in December 1864.

09-134 | manuscript
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf | PDF scan page 134
09-134-P01
There is a Schooner at the landing on the bayou, just in from Tampico laden with merchandise. It belongs to [[Reichman?]] and Myers of this city.
Quite a number keep out of the Service along the coast by blockade running, though they do not run on them themselves. A few men are around gathering conscripts and forwarding them to the front, they had better be gathering up loose & useless officers and putting them where they belong instead of bothering honest men.
As it is late and cold having no fire in our room I will Close. I have to take this to the P.O tonight So it will get off in the morning to Millican.
With best love to all
I remain Your brother
Geo Douglas.

EDITORIAL NOTE: Conclusion of 09-129–133, dated December 11, 1864. First merchant’s name is tentative. Claims about avoiding military service are the writer’s opinion, not a verified finding concerning every merchant or shipowner named.

10-045 | poem
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf | PDF scan page 45
10-045-P01
154
Parody.

10-045-P02
’Tis the first rose of Summer
Fresh blooming and fair
Which sheds its sweet fragrance
Upon the soft air;
Oh! how sweetly it blushes
Like a young maiden’s cheek
When emotions are burning
The lip cannot speak.

10-045-P03
I’ll not leave thee, thou fair one
To bloom on the stem,
But will gather thee gently
The days sweetest gem;
While the dewdrop yet lingers
Upon thy bright leaves;
As the tear on the lashes
When th’heart fondly grieves.

10-045-P04
And soon will I give thee
In Friendship’s true name
To one who will prize thee
Through life still the same;
True hearts ne’er are withered
Tho’ Youth’s bloom be gone
And that Love is immutable
Where Friendship first shone.

10-045-P05
April 1868.

EDITORIAL NOTE: Manuscript page 154. No author’s signature appears on this page. The heading “Parody” is retained without supplying an external source or attribution.

10-046 | poem
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf | PDF scan page 46
10-046-P01
153
To Emma.
Of Zephyrus Bower,—By “Moore” the second.

10-046-P02
Part First.
Awake my sweet Lyre
To Love I aspire
Pure as the desire
Of Angels above
Hopes which I cherish
Never let perish
And cast a dark gloom
O’er Fancy’s first bloom
But live forever
And flow as a river
A torrent of Love.
Then welcome the hour
It finds Emma’s bower
Where by thy sweet power
I’m carried along;
The Muses around
Enchant The fair ground
With Music’s sweet sound
A heavenly Song.
Then joy so complete
While at Emma’s feet
I softly repeat
And for each word vouch
That fondly I love her
By all that’s above her
And will till times over
My dear Emma Couch.

10-046-P03
Part Second
Awake my sweet Lyre
Affections desire
A heavenly fire
Courses my veins
Oh! let thy sweet sound
Come floating around
With gentle rebound
In melodious strains;
For Emma divine
Will never be mine
Unless I can shine
By Poesy’s power.
For no other score
Will I go before
A second “Tom Moore”
To zephyrus bower,
But that me will raise
I fondly surmise
And in Emma’s eyes
Perhaps may succeed
Then Life will be bright
And joyous and light,
And in young Love’s sight
Elysium indeed.

10-046-P04
Part Third.
Awake my sweet Lyre
You know my desire;
Oh! now go and fire
Another young heart
Thus you will prove
That you can wake Love
In Bower or Grove
Wherever you start.
Let Love’s sweetest Song
Thy cadence prolong
While moving along
That verdant bower
Whose perfumes shaken
Emma will waken
[[separate block: final two lines in the right margin]]
To live the peerless
Maid of thy bower.

EDITORIAL NOTE: Manuscript page 153, in two columns. Part Second runs from the bottom of the left column to the top of the right; Part Third ends in two rotated margin lines. “Moore” the second and “Tom Moore” are the poem’s own descriptions, not a verified attribution. “times over” is reproduced as written. The text names Emma Couch, but neither her identity nor a historical relationship is established here.

10-047 | poem
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf | PDF scan page 47
10-047-P01
Bachelor’s Lament.
July 1875

10-047-P02
O! where is the hope of the vine covered cottage
The visions of Youth will so oft conjure up
Forever ’tis gone, and now gray in my dotage
I’ve drained to the dregs Life’s bitterest cup.
And where is the dear One I’ve loved with devotion
Thro’ life’s changeful scenes of unhallowed commotion
With ever the same constant and changeless emotion
Beloved at the first and beloved to the close.

10-047-P03
No answer comes back from my voiceless surroundings
For silence and gloom are my comrades alway,
I’m sad as if sunk ’neath the Sea’s deepest Soundings
Where the [[deleted: uncoffined dead]] [[inserted: dead of the past]] lie mould’ring away,
O! when will this cease here, this dread desolation
Which binds my soul down in its deep tribulation
And is there no season of calm consolation
No morning unfolding again as the rose?

10-047-P04
Alone now I wander on life’s rugged byways
The friends of my Youth I may never greet more
For many have fallen on far distant highways
And beckon me on to the Stygian shore;
And ’neath yon low mound where the willow stands weeping
My heart’s only darling forever is sleeping
O! may the Death Angel make haste with his reaping
And gather me there to a dreamless repose!

10-047-P05
Forever shall cease then those ties that are breaking
And sweetly I’ll rest in the calm of the tomb.
No storms can assail ’till the morn of awaking
Shall beckon the dead back to joy or gloom—
Around me shall linger no omen of danger
Which compassed my way while a sad lonely ranger
To all save a Peace—deep and dreamless a Stranger
There calmly I’ll rest from my life’s gloomy woes.

EDITORIAL NOTE: A clearer version of passages also present in the faint notebook drafts at 10-021 and 10-026. The interlinear revision in stanza two is shown explicitly. No signature is visible. The poem’s references to aging, a lost beloved, and death are literary statements; they do not by themselves establish the author’s age, marital status, or a named person’s death.

10-049 | poem
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf | PDF scan page 49
10-049-P01
74
To Victoria.

10-049-P02
Welcome Victoria! to Brushy’s green slopes
The Cradle and Grave of my Bachelor hopes
Here they opened and flourished and fell in decay
As flowers nipt by a frost in the genial May.

10-049-P03
But why should I trouble you with Sorrows of Mine!
For thousands have felt them, and thousands repine
But may the kind Angel who is guarding thy way
Protect you from them wherever you Stray.

10-049-P04
Thrice happy the hours since to Brushy you came
For enjoyments exist now which were only a name;
And sweeter than roses the converse we hold
And the swift flying moments are brighter than gold.

10-049-P05
I speak not of Love, that fountain is dry
Deception and Falsehood have quenched its supply
Experience has taught me, the daughters of Eve
The fairest the brightest were born to deceive.

10-049-P06
Sweet Ida was fickle, but still in my heart
Her image is graven and will never depart,
But Inez with falsehood has stained her young fame
And the curse of a Douglas now rests on her name.

10-049-P07
Tell me why should the truthful one sympathy hold
For that glittering dross which alloys the gold
Or what what concord has night with the morn of the day
The glow worms cold glare with the sun’s gentle ray.

EDITORIAL NOTE: Manuscript page 74. Continued at 10-048 (manuscript page 75), where the poem is dated July 1875. The repeated “what what” is retained. “A Douglas” appears in the poem, but it is not an author’s signature. Brushy is not assigned to a specific modern location here. The accusations about Ida, Inez, and women generally are the speaker’s rhetoric, not independently verified statements.

10-050 | poem
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf | PDF scan page 50
10-050-P01
13
On the Banks of Brushy.

10-050-P02
Fair Brushy! again beside thy winding stream
I rove again as in my childhood’s days
And with ardor dream again each early dream
Which once beguiled my young artless ways;
O’er them still my Memory fondly strays
Sweet treasures of the Past forever fled
And doomed to rot in dark Oblivion’s maze
Where all that’s pure and bright is tending fast
To mingle with Earth’s common clay at last.

10-050-P03
Here first I heard the sky-lark’s warbling notes
As it high ascended from its dewy nest:
And here from a thousand other funny throats
I heard the tones which swelled each tender breast
Rising to Heaven as though they blest
The great Creator’s name with guileless heart
Who had all things in such beauty drest
And given them here fair Freedom’s part
Unstained by Man, with his dark wily art.

10-050-P04
Here too I culled the lovely flowers which grew
In rich profusion on each verdant lawn
Adding their charms of every varied hue
Which could not be restored when they were gone
Then with listless steps I wandered on
To seek for others still more sweet
Until the approach of evening’s dawn
Homeward turned my wandering feet
From many a pleasant flower adorned retreat.

10-050-P05
But ere from each pleasant landscape I withdrew
I culled from many a lone mossy glen
The lovely violets which in rich profusion grew
In every woodland brake and tangled fen—

EDITORIAL NOTE: Manuscript page 13, continuing at 10-051 (page 14). “Funny throats” and “evening’s dawn” are retained as written. The speaker’s childhood landscape is called Brushy, but the poem alone does not securely identify either its author or the geographical location. The complete identified reading order is 10-050, 10-051, 10-060, 10-061, 10-052, 10-053 (manuscript pages 13–18).

10-051 | poem continuation
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf | PDF scan page 51
10-051-P01
14
And naming each for earth’s illustrious men
And counting signal numbers for each side,
Vigorously began the mock battle—and when
The flowery fight was done—and all but one had died
O’er that Last victor my heart thrilled in boyish pride

10-051-P02
To think that I like it would triumph over all
Who were arrayed against me as my foes
That I would thus witness the last one fall
Whom my right of sway would ever dare oppose.
And of my life victory and peace would be the close
Was the emblem which I saw in that flower
And did not note how soon it died with those
It had o’erthrown in battle’s stormy hour
Yielding with them all unto a mightier power.

10-051-P03
But as those lovely flowers withering died
Together in one fragrant floral heap
So perished those early joys which were allied
Unto the future where broad Fancy’s sweep
Grasped the immortal and bade me keep
An erect brow through swiftly coming years
And clamber up Fame’s long wished steep
Whose shaggy brow in the dim future rears
Aloft above the rabble’s taunting jeers.

10-051-P04
But still those early scenes in freshness bloom
Those brighter fancies of my childhood’s time
Shine from afar, though intervening gloom
And the wide distance gives them doubly the sublime
Of Beauty, Glory, and Grandeur, which in their prime
They wore unto my young enraptured eyes,
As the measured feet of impassioned rhyme
Lends dignity unto the writings of the wise
Which Clothed in Poetry more majestically rise.

EDITORIAL NOTE: Manuscript page 14 continues 10-050 (page 13). It continues at 10-060 (page 15), then 10-061 (page 16), 10-052 (page 17), and 10-053 (page 18). The flower battle is explicitly a child’s game, not an account of a military engagement.

10-052-P01

But once more the sun is in the glowing east,
Once more the day has come beautiful and bright,
Once more from Sweet Slumber’s bond released
All Nature hails the grand return of Light.
Once more unto my eager ravished sight
The dew drops sparkle brightly on a thousand flowers
From the pure crimson to the spotless white
Which richly glow in Nature’s vernal bowers
Adding sweetest perfumes to the returning hours.

10-052-P02
The lowing herds wandering forth to crop the grass
O’er mead and hill in boundless pastures free
The soft tinkling bells upon them as they pass
Ringing on the morning air so merrily,
And in a thousand brakes the song birds cheerily
Hymning on High their Sweet discordant notes
All forming [[deleted: the sweetest]] [[inserted: a Sweeter]] chorus [[deleted: which]] [[inserted: than]] ever we
Have heard from any choirs of well trained throats
As it through the Soft air, gently heavenward floats

10-052-P03
But the hour for School has come, we must along
With Satchel and basket, and beneath the teachers eye
Con our lessons over with a hum-drum Song
With many a furtive glance at the bright blue sky
And longing from the close School-room to fly
To the cooling Stream or groves deep vernal shade
Or o’er the flowery plain to chase the butterfly
Where thro’ the long hours of morning it has Strayed
Sipping the sweet from the flowers where it has played.

10-052-P04
Hail glorious playtime! for awhile set free
With wild shouts we hail thee in the open air
Happy as any class of mortals well can be
Having to pleasure now our odd hour to spare,

EDITORIAL NOTE: Manuscript page 17 follows the displaced pages 15 and 16 at 10-060 and 10-061. The final stanza continues at 10-053 (page 18). Revisions in the birdsong stanza are recorded rather than silently discarded.

10-053 | poem continuation
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf | PDF scan page 53
10-053-P01
18
And laying aside every thought and care
Which jocund joy might possibly impede
And dividing into equal sides prepare
For boyish games; and firing to nought else heed
With laugh and shout the winged hours we speed.

10-053-P02
Thrice happy time! with no foreboding cares opprest
The glowing hours in joy are winged away
And present Hopes with full fruition blest
Portend no shadows in Lifes evening day.
Alas! that those should ever o’er us stray
To blight young Friendship in the early bud
And drown their first purest blessed joy
Beneath dark Detractions turbid flood—
Whose boiling tide inundates all that’s good.

10-053-P03
Oh! why should the Schoolboys path of flowers
Be lined with thorns at every step he treads?
Oh! why should his Life’s young gladsome bowers
Conceal that Serpent in their floral beds
Whose poisonous fangs obscured in hydra heads
Of hate, malice, Scorn, Contempt, and pride,
Strike with all their venom natively inbred
Until the nobler passions of the heart have died
Or with the baseness of Lucifer allied.

EDITORIAL NOTE: Manuscript page 18 continues the playtime stanza at 10-052. “Firing” appears in the line about paying no heed and is retained, although “giving” would be expected in context. The complete identified reading order is 10-050, 10-051, 10-060, 10-061, 10-052, 10-053 (manuscript pages 13–18).

Things I Love
Written for Miss Ida;

10-054-P02
I love to love all lovely things
From which the charm of Beauty [[springs?]]
To captivate the heart,
From lichens on the mountain crest
To lowly vales in sunlight drest
The high, the lowly part,
The Hero’s proud and pompous sway
The Senate’s stern command,
The Ploughman’s noteless little day,
The humblest in our land,
The grandly great, the low-[[illegible]]
Alike possess a charm
There’s Splendor there, And Beauty here
To keep the life blood warm,

10-054-P03
The mutual pledge and mutual trust
Are joys which time can never rust
Nor lessen in degree
They spring from heart to kindred heart
And form of Life the sweeter part
Whose [[joys?]] never flee
Forms may decay, and friends grow strange
And lovely objects fly,
And Time’s mute step, with silent change
May bid the fairest die
But these will e’er remain to cheer
Tho’ all beside are gone
And Life be bright with roseate light,
With one perpetual dawn,

10-055 | poem continuation
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf | PDF scan page 55
10-055-P01
63
Soon shall we pass away, nor leave behind
To tell what we have been, a single trace
Like some frail gossamer wafted by the wind
We’ll go, and none may ever mark the place
Where we shall fall. Life’s eager busy race
Will have no time to pause. When we are gone
The young the gay will laugh around, the chase
Of Life’s vain [[phantoms?]], still will lead them on
Until they too with us, shall try the Great Beyond.

10-055-P02
Flow on thou River, Still flow on. The Sea
Will welcome thee to its deep dark abyss,
Thy course is marked, and I can [[mark?]] in Thee
The type of Human Life. Nor can we miss
The doom awaiting us, The woe, the bliss
Of that last hour, to which we all must come
And there resign the pomp the fame of this
In the deep sleep of our last quiet [[illegible]]
Till called to swell the throng in yon eternal dome.

10-055-P03
June 1874.

And too, I love the friendly flow,

Who bow beneath the hand of God
And smile thro’ tears and kiss the rod
Ere yet the blow is given,
Lone Pilgrims still, and strangers here
Amid a world of strife
With practice pure, and conscience clear
Their title deed to [[Life?]],
With living Faith that conquers death
A high and holy trust
They calmly wait, the last [[mandate?]]
“Thou Shalt return to dust”

10-056-P03
Feby 1873

Who will not pause to note the bliss
That springs from raptured scenes [[ideal?]]
Is dead to all that’s dear,
In vain the seasons may return
The Poles may freeze and Tropics [[burn?]]
Alike to him the year,
The flowers which strew the prairies green
May make a mute appeal
The Choral grove,—the Sylvan Scene
All—cannot make him feel,
But still can I each rapture Spy,
That springs on plain or spray;
And love them still, with earnest will
The gentle and the gay.

10-057-P02

I’m sure a raptured thrill [[has been?]]
Down there awhile to stay,
I’ll gather then the nameless sweet
From out each lone obscure [[retreat?]]
Half hidden from the day,
For still the mead and mountains brow
Their varied beauties [[yield?]],—
The Summer’s bloom, and Winter’s snow
Still give me joys annealed,
With eager grasp, each one I clasp,
With grateful throbbing heart
I love them all, the great and [[small?]]
The rapture giving part.

10-059 | poem
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf | PDF scan page 59
10-059-P01
61
Apostrophe To the Brazos.

10-059-P02
Sweet Brazos! Still thy murmuring waters lave
Thy pebbly strand beneath yon Mountain height
Whose summit crowned by an ancient Indian [[inserted: grave]]
At once his nation’s pride and nation’s might,
Some hundred years have winged their weary flight
Since he was laid within the warriors tomb
O! what a change hath been! What withering blight
Has stamped the red man with an early doom—
And swept him from the earth, to give the pale face room.

10-059-P03
But still thou flowest on as in days of yore
With the same old tones, within thy Rocky bed
The rugged cliffs still crown thy winding shore—
Perchance an aged tree still rears its head;
And saving these, all [[other?]] Scenes have fled,
The Warrior proud and strong—his dusky Bride
The stalwart Chief—and trusted Steed—are dead
The Wigwam gone—with all the Red Man’s pride
Swept with the flying years, [[illegible]] from their changeful tide.

10-059-P04
Though these are gone, still hearts as fondly brave
And deeply true, still beat along thy stream,
As those, thy long gone primal ages gave,
Unto the world, and still as [[vainly?]] dream
Of Love and Happiness, and fondly deem
That they in after years will grasp the wand
Of Human Bliss, whose rich illusive gleam
Seen from afar but vainly leads them on
Till Youth and health and strength and hope and life are gone.

10-059-P05
Tho’ this be so, O! still we’ll grasp the hour
That beams with Love and Hope’s illusive smile
We’ll woo its presence, and its cheerful power
To be around us, tho’ for so short awhile

EDITORIAL NOTE: Manuscript page 61. Read 10-059, 10-058, 10-055 (manuscript pages 61–63); the conclusion is dated June 1874. “Grave” is inserted above the first stanza. The poem imagines an Indigenous grave and presents a nineteenth-century narrative of Indigenous disappearance. Neither the grave’s identity or age nor the claim of disappearance is independently established by this poem. No tribal identity or precise landmark is supplied.

10-060-P01

Thus still those early scenes which first I knew
Linger on the pages of the shadowy Past
Which as Memory turns its leaves comes to view
In pure unstained colors, which will last
When the bands of Age are round me cast
And earthly joys grow dim and fade away
And Life’s last sands are ebbing fast
And soon to mingle with earth’s common clay
Where all at last must moulder and decay.

10-060-P02
How beautiful! when the garish day was done
The sky appeared in twilight’s lovely hue
When the last lingering rays of the glorious sun
With amber streaked the deep heavenly blue
Unto my boyish eyes the glorious view
Seemed but the portals of a heaven on high
Where from the horizon we might spring through
And taste immortal bliss above the sky
With those pure Spirits there which never die.

10-060-P03
And as still deeper glowed the tints of night
Upon that horizon’s far distant west.
The stars came forth with their lovely light
And gazed on the earth like Spirits blest
Watching it whilst it calmly sank to rest
From the toil and cares of days passed here
Whose fierce pursuits, pursued with eager zest
By men, seeking for some altitude of power
To dispense to mankind, curses by the hour.

10-060-P04
How softly falls, with the calm advance of night
Its mild influences on mans stormy soul!
Erasing the stripes of day, and bearing [[unsought?]]
That boon of Heaven, whose high goal

10-061 | poem continuation
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf | PDF scan page 61
10-061-P01
16
Is fixed where Time’s billows can never roll
Nor reach with their canker and decay
The immortal Spirit’s far magnetic pole
Around which it pursues its eternal way
In the boundless light of an unending day.

10-061-P02
At length when all without was calm and still
I would seek in slumber deep for childhood’s dream
Softly lulled to sleep by the lone whip-poor-will
Which sang its sweet song in nights soft beams
And which to my young imaginations seems
A lovely creature sent with pure nameless charms
And matchless beauty, which in the starlight gleams
Brilliant and bright, such as mightily warms
A poets fancy when wrapped in Morpheus’ arms.

10-061-P03
How quiet are childhood’s slumbers! how free from all
The stormy dreams of manhood’s feverish sleep!
No wild unrest, no vain ambitions lofty fall!
No withering hopes! o’er which to wake and weep
But all is peace, and soft repose—and sweetly keep
Their star watch o’er the young and tender frame
Now resting in sweet unconsciousness so deep,
That ’twere a pity, it should ever wake to claim
A place again on the rough road to earthly Fame.

10-061-P04
Oh! it were better far in our earliest days
Before we learn the torturing way of Sin,
That in Death, should be quenched Life’s loved bright rays
And we, sink into the tomb—though cold within
Should be its cold vault—yet Oh! ’tis there
Through that drear portal, and break the chain
Of icy bondage there—and triumphing in
The death struggle—returned unto Heaven again
Resting the bliss of victory and Death of pain.

EDITORIAL NOTE: Manuscript page 16 follows 10-060 and precedes 10-052. This locates the two manuscript pages displaced from the poem’s earlier scan sequence. The closing stanza is syntactically difficult; its words and line divisions are preserved without rewriting the archival text into smoother theology. The final phrase appears to be “Resting the bliss,” not silently changed to “Tasting.”

10-065 | poem

10-065-P01

To Miss M. L. G.......

10-065-P02
Now gentle peace has come again
And every girl wants a man
And every man is in a whirl
Looking around for a girl
Who is to share his after life
As his companion—partner—wife—
And all is bustle and confusion
Around Hymen’s bower—and the allusion,
To anything that ties up two
For life in bonds enduring
In a young chap will never do
That is if he is not a “daring.”

10-065-P03
But as each one has some choice above
The ordinary feelings of his mind
I sincerely think the “Elm Grove”
Will fill the Ideal to which I’m inclined.
And I do intend to win
The prize that there is glowing
But doubtless I’ll have opposition in
My endeavors at so doing.
I know of but only four
Who stand opposed to my endeavors
Yet they may puzzle me quite sore
As, They are gentlemanly and clever,
I will mention them in detail
And pardon any digression
That may occur in manner metrical
For this is an allowed transgression.

EDITORIAL NOTE: Manuscript page 5, on a reused military form. Continues through 10-066–10-068, ending with a May 1, 1866 date. “Elm Grove” and the four rivals’ labels are left as the poem presents them; no identities or modern place locations are inferred. Hymen’s bower is an image of marriage. The light, competitive rhetoric does not establish actual engagements.

So will you not come and stay
Forever there with it.

10-068-P02
My misery is complete on earth
Alone as I am living
My life is a very death
To me no pleasure giving.
Shortly then I know I’ll die
Because no one will me love
The reason I cannot tell why,
Can you fair maid of “Elm Grove”

10-068-P03
I loved you at first and now still better
And love you I ever will
This you may see by my letter
Can you love a Verdant Hill?

10-068-P04
May 1st 1866

10-070 | prose essay
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf | PDF scan page 70
10-070-P01
10
[[separate block: preprinted descriptive roll and enlistment headings, as at 10-068]]
Social Parties—What Are They?

10-070-P02
The Social Parties as practiced by the Native and Adopted citizens of the younger class in this Section are in my humble opinion the most ridiculous amusements which it is possible for intelligent people to practice. Imagine a gathering of thirty or forty young people aged respectively from eighteen to thirty at some place selected for the contemplated performance. Having met and sat about rather indolently for awhile apparently very much embarrassed and seemingly very modest and very fearful of doing something contrary to the rules of Etiquette some venturesome character proposes a “play” The young gents capering select their partners and ere long promenading the floor in a circle by twos to the bewitching strains of “Old Sister Phebe” or “My pretty little love” or some other popular air sung in enchanting style by some one or two vocalists. No conversation worthy the name is ever carried on by any couple, those not engaged in singing keep profoundly silent or indulge in unmeasured laughter at some real or imaginary blunders of some one or more of the party. Tiring of the first or any other play each individual looks for a seat for him or herself, or a drink of water or something else. The girls congregate on one side of the house and indulge in apparently very lively and interesting chat if we are to judge from the many Smiling faces and little giggles which may from time

EDITORIAL NOTE: Manuscript page 10 continues at 10-071. This is the writer’s satirical criticism, not a neutral survey. The location and date become explicit on the following page: Ellis County, Texas, May 1866. “Native and Adopted citizens” here distinguishes local-born residents and newcomers in the writer’s wording; it is not an identification of Indigenous ancestry. Song titles are transcribed, not attributed to an external version.

Common sense could suggest many convenient ways of amusement which would be [[profitable as well as agreeable?]].

10-073 | personal reflection
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf | PDF scan page 73
10-073-P01
13
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
A residence of Sixteen years in this portion of Texas (Ellis County) has not made me fall in love with it by any means. ’Tis may be the easiest place to “get along” in of any other—yet the experience which I have had here in common farming life forces me to the conclusion that it is a hard place to make a living. The general mildness of the climate, and [[slowness?]] of the Summer have enervated the inhabitants to such a degree that they do not look forward with the proper foresight in regard to their pecuniary interests. Proper places for deposit of grain are not provided and frequently crops suffer [[deleted: from]] destruction to a considerable extent from this cause alone. We are poorly provided with machinery of all descriptions, There is not half mills enough in the country consequently instead of Competition we have Combination, and exorbitant rates of toll are charged which is detrimental to the farming interests of the country, but we farmers have to submit to an [[illegible]] which we cannot help and any hope [[illegible]] away change. I cite Millers [[illegible]] which [[inflict?]] upon the Community—Other professions do likewise as far as they are able. Self is the governing principle here [[to?]] the exclusion of all other and [[while?]] [[illegible]] [[localities?]] whose competition gives the farming class a chance to realize the full value of their crops from year to year [[would?]] surely be more desirable than [[illegible]] they are much the most [[illegible]].

EDITORIAL NOTE: Manuscript page 13 is unsigned and undated. The preceding page is dated July 4, 1866; this does not establish this page’s date or author. Sixteen years is an explicit statement, but a circa-1850 arrival would be an inference contingent on dating and identification. The writer’s opinions about climate, inhabitants and millers are not independently verified. The lower portion is faded and several connecting clauses remain unreadable.

10-074 | prose essay
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf | PDF scan page 74
10-074-P01
14
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
Home

10-074-P02
There are many pleasant associations connected with the word Home, It embodies at one group and in one view the leading features of our earlier days. Our first recollections, our first associations our first connections all spring at once to the mind at the mention of that one word. Our recollections of the innocent Sports that beguiled the days of our infancy, when lighthearted and joyous we played amid Sunshine and flowers, inhaling the wild free air and Spirit of nature, careless and gay as the bright plumaged birds which warbled their hymns of praise from every tree, Free as they from the follies and vices of the world nor dreaming of the blight of after years through which we would be called to pass—Our earlier associations with companions joyous as we, which can never be renewed, but which will linger in Memory, as one of the brightest periods of our existence; and to which we can always turn with pleasing emotions—Our earlier connections with parents, brothers, and sisters, fond endearing ties, woven in childhood years, and never to be forgotten, though separated by time and distance, far from the places where they sprung into existence—These remembrances all spring within the mind when Home is mentioned and as we contemplate them through the lapse of years they assume a hallowed purity, which no other scenes or associations can. They are holy because they belong to the past, they are sacred because they are pure and uncontaminated by vile connections, they are the tender ties of early love, mutually enjoyed and mutually reciprocated, they are the holy links which bind the family

EDITORIAL NOTE: Manuscript page 14 continues at 10-075. This is a general reflection, not a list of the writer’s own identified relatives. The following page says it was written at a young lady’s request at Seclusion, September 20, 1866.

10-075-P02
Sonnet or, Blent Flowers,
Adieu ye bright hopes that so fondly have hovered
Around the light dreams of my earlier days
When with feelings transparent and affections uncovered
I faced the gay world in its meridian blaze
Those visions of joy bright [[deleted: in]] [[inserted: all]] ecstatic Elysian
Have faded before adversity’s cold gaze
And nought now remains but those dreams [[deleted: of]] [[inserted: Life’s elysion]]
Dimly discovered through memory’s dark haze
But still they will linger on those dim distant pages
And occasionally be read when a sunbeam there strays
And fondly remembered as one of those happy ages
That in Childhood and Youth deceivingly plays
But will return not again in life’s varied stages
Although we hope for it in Philosophy’s atherian ways
Seclusion July 1866

To W. H. B.....

10-076-P02
Though short the time since first we met
The few bright and glowing scenes
That have past I can never forget
While I know what pleasure means.
But to those moments sweetly fraught
That yielded such a pleasant time
I would bestow a passing thought
Penned in idle Scattering rhyme.

10-076-P03
To Friendship I would dedicate my verse
(That brightly blooms in darkest hours)
And though it may be rude and coarse
A nobler aim shall direct its powers.

10-076-P04
May the friendship we have just begun
Stand the test of after years
“And round our hearts be surely spun”
The chains that pleasure fondly bears,

10-076-P05
True Friendship like the gnarled Oak
Firm rooted in the rock
Feel the lightnings deadliest Stroke
And brave the tempests rudest shock,
But when the moaning storms are sped,
And calmly comes the hour of even—
Again it rears its vernal head
Towards the ether vault of Heaven,

10-076-P06
Be it ours to brave the lightnings brand
Of malice dark and dread,

10-078 | comic poem
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf | PDF scan page 78
10-078-P01
18
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
To the Y. L. of the L. S.
(Or the gnawing of a bone)

10-078-P02
Now gentle girls polite and fair
As I am tonight all alone
I will try and get off some rhyming ware
About a tough and crusty bone.

10-078-P03
I am told you have a bone to gnaw
Harder than any heretofore known
The like of it nobody ever saw
It is such a very strange bone.

10-078-P04
Every monday morning I understand
All of your faults you have to own
Then lay strong hold with both your hands
And go to gnawing on this bone.

10-078-P05
Tewsday comes bright and fair
Yet there is no softness shown
And each moment you busy are
Gnawing away upon this bone.

10-078-P06
So you go until Saturday
The trying task all week youve known
Yet you have not gnawed away
One particle of this hard bone.

10-078-P07
Then comes the Sabbath pure and bright
Its glories over earth are thrown

EDITORIAL NOTE: Manuscript page 18 begins a comic poem continued through 10-080, dated Seclusion, December 8, 1866. Initials are not expanded with certainty. The bone becomes an insult to a person in the final stanza; its gnawing imagery is figurative.

The like of it I have never known
’Tis neither smooth nor very rough
Possibly it may be your bone?

10-079-P03
When I used to be in the army
I ate everything to me thrown
For I knew it could not harm me
Although it was a dry bone.

10-079-P04

For it makes my teeth ache, I own,
And I do not like the bliss
There is in gnawing on this bone.

10-079-P05

Or anything I have ever known
So I will look over the world wide
To find a name for this bone.

10-079-P06
’Tis neither duck nor goose nor chick
Nor of no hog with fat oer grown
But something mighty hard and Slick
So I am sure it is a bone.

10-079-P07
’Tis not sheep nor deer nor horse
Nor anything in modern times grown
So I think as a matter of course

10-082 | love poem
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf | PDF scan page 82
10-082-P01
22
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
To Miss M. A. A.

10-082-P02
When Heavens blue arch so gracefully bending
Above me brightly glows with loves azure hue
And the mind with sweet thoughts calmly ascending
Along that bright arch turns fair Mary to you.

10-082-P03
As the needle with magnet faithfully thrilling
Still points to the pole so steady and true
So the deepest emotions of my hearts fond instilling
Drawn with true magnet fair Mary to you.

10-082-P04
And when on the green grassy banks reclining
Of fair Red Oak, listening to its waters flowing there
The entrancing shades, above it so gracefully entwining
Fond Memory turns fair Mary to you.

10-082-P05
The voices of waters songsters in those bowers dwellying
My wild restless Spirit does enchantingly woo
But still while I listen to the wild choral ringing
In rapture my heart turns fair Mary to you.

10-082-P06
And like the Sunflower its fair face Extending
In the early morn ere it sheds the bright dew
To meet the bold gaze of its bright god ascending
So I open my heart fair Mary to you.

10-082-P07
In the morning of Life I am now joyously standing
Before me is spread bright prospects sweet to view
With the gay Charm of Hope my heart is expanding
But they all point at last fair Mary to—you.

EDITORIAL NOTE: Manuscript page 22 continues through 10-084, where it is signed Geo. Douglas, Seclusion, October 15, 1866. Mary is named in the poem; her remaining initials are not expanded. “Red Oak” is named as a watercourse in the poem. Unusual syntax, such as “Drawn with true magnet,” is retained.

That afflicts us when we love the lovely and true

As those I have felt fair Mary for you.

10-085-P03
Now the lark from [[inserted: its]] dewy nest widely Springing
Soars far up on high oer the green coated plain
And amid the blue heavens sweetly is Singing
In the ear of its Maker natures wild strain,
In his viewless wake, my Soul I am flinging
Robed in a vesture of fair heavenly hue
And with the “music of the Spheres” my Spirit is ringing
Commingling their sweetness fair Mary for you.
Nov 186[[lost: remaining date at right edge]]

10-085-P04
From Heavens high portals Angels are descending
Bearing their harps of bright golden hue—
To meet the bright host on Faiths wings ascending
My Spirit traverses the Skys ether blue.
Ten thousand voices in harmony blending
Bequeathed me an offering beautiful and true
Of Love in its brightness, all things Earthly, transcending
And bade me bear it fair Mary to you.
Jan 27–1867

EDITORIAL NOTE: Manuscript page 25 continues “To the Same” from 10-084. A date at the right edge reads Nov 186 followed by loss; it is not completed conjecturally. The following stanza has the separate date January 27, 1867. Some unusual phrasing, including “ranging hopes,” is retained.

10-086 | satirical poem
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf | PDF scan page 86
10-086-P01
26
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
Dutch Campmeeting 1866.
In 1866 in September
I went to the campmeeting
And as well as I can remember
Received a very cordial greeting
The first of social joys which I took
Was a gentle sprinkling.
Thus I caught a forward look
And of what was coming got an inkling.
’Twas rain a shower and mud a heap
And drabbled dresses plenty
And I got many a sly peep
At tapering ankles from ten to twenty.
The camp accommodations were very poor
And it did not suit the lasses
To have to sit upon the floor
On straw in lieu of grasses.
Grasses they would have preferred beneath a willow
Soft yielding green dewy sparkling ever
And every lass of them a handsome fellow
To twain bright garland posies weaving ever
But alas! the difference, a preacher here
Restraining the free flow of chat
Between the gents and ladies fair
A thing they all would fain be at.
But after a while they bolder grew
And some got in the passage
And what do ye think they did do
When they got the passage?
Why they mixed all up together
In a crowd huddle—

EDITORIAL NOTE: Manuscript page 26 begins a long satirical poem continued through 10-090. “To twain bright garland posies weaving ever” is unusual wording retained as read. The social and physical descriptions are the speaker’s often unkind judgments. This verse should not be treated as a verified report about identifiable people.

10-088 | satirical poem continuation

How affectionate they looked so coy and sly
With their bright eyes glancing about
Seeming to say “if you will but try
The kisses you may have with a pout!”
By hokey! the favorite young devil
Who was smart enough to get a few smacks
Should I find him in manner quite civil
I’ll endeavor to walk in his tracks!
I will be all smiles and attention
And specially notice their slightest needs
Do everything that politeness could mention
And think of all things that it cant.
And always with the greatest deference
Will I lift my hat when I speak to them
And always manifest the greatest preference
For any thing to which they take the whim.
To please them so in a loving mood
I will tell them lies by the score
And if this does not do any good
I will tell them twice as many more.
Then if I see their brows gently reproving
I will instantly recant all I have said
And be so affectionate and loving
They will bestow blessings by the forewarning head,
In short I will bend as the willow
To every slight breath of the wind
And do everything in the world to pillow
My head on their bosoms so kind!

10-088-P02
But I know there are some peevish creatures
Who long since have lost their lovely features

Fit sequel to his lifes deep seated gloom.

The wild enchanting raptures tell
Of the wide world exists all in this.
Sept 1866

10-091 | reflective poem
Source: George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf | PDF scan page 91
10-091-P01
31
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
Idle Hours.

10-091-P02
I can for hours watch the tempest fly
And listen to the deep mouthed thunder roar
As they roll in grandeur in the sky
Where all was peace and quiet once before.

10-091-P03
And a wild companionship I own
With these fierce scenes of strife,
Now that my serener peace is gone
In the rude blasts of early life.

10-091-P04
Once was my sky bright blue and clear
And every hope of pleasure gave
But now alas! all is dull and drear
And fondest hopes lie withered in the grave.

10-091-P05
What once was spread with fairest flowers
And where sweetest fruit in prospect gleamed
When pleasure winged the golden hours
And light and life and joy all seemed
To be upon my pathway bright spread
With happiness the vision bright
All fraught with bliss before me laid
In one long line of gleaming light.

10-091-P06
I little dreamed of this dark hour
When Peace I’d woo from wildest strife
Or thought I’d subject be to the dark power
Which blasted thus my early life

EDITORIAL NOTE: Manuscript page 31 continues at the top of 10-092, dated Seclusion, August 23, 1866. “What once” and the unusual syntax of the longer stanza are retained. The poem’s buried hopes and blighted life are figurative statements, not proof of a named bereavement.

I face the world nor fear its scorn
Conscious still that I can bear my part
Though deeper in my bosom press the thorn.
Seclusion Aug 23rd 1866

10-092-P02
[[separate block: a second poem, main text continuing into the lower right margin]]
While backward gazing through the lapse of years
A lone oasis in my early life appears
Beautifully verdured and flowery fair
And draped in brightness richly rare
There Sunshine played o’er [[inserted: each]] happy scene
And enchanting beauties shed their silver sheen
Upon the vernal air, in bright relief
To Lifes surrounding wastes of gloomy grief.

10-092-P03
Careless I strayed its glorious aisles among
Where mid embowering sweets still sweeter sung
Innocent warblers their soul stirring lays
Adding music’s bliss to each unclouding maze—
Blinded by the beauteous scenes I saw around
Methought these scenes so bright would always abound
That downward in Life’s meandering march
Such beauteous bowers would forever arch
Amid my pathway and lend their brightest hues
To shed a soft delight and milder joys infuse.

10-092-P04

And before me lay Lifes dreary waste
Its scorching sands far spread before the eye
Where fierce Simoons of Hate hurl them on high
Burying beneath its fiercely burning sway
Each nobler passion that might chance to stray
Oft in the desert heart where once sweetly stood
All the purer instincts of the generously good,
But where nought now of pleasures hopes remains
Except the sad Remembrance—“it can ne’er come again!”
Jan 14th 1867
George Douglas

10-092-P05

There is a loneliness of the heart
No words can e’er express
Too deep for Sorrows tears to start
To relieve the aching breast
A joyless motionless [[moodly?]] waste
All dark and drear, forlorn
And every lovely flower thats placed
Upon it hides a poisonous thorn.
G. D.

[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
Idle Hours.

10-097-P02
The first the fondest purest hopes
Of Lifes bright sunny hour
Bloom fresh within a narrow scope
Like Springs bright vernal flower.

10-097-P03
Then does the mind expanding glow
Beneath a genial Sun
And joys bright perennial flow
Yet still their source is one.

10-097-P04
That source is guileless innocence
By the infant heart expressed
Breathing a holy sweet incense
Upon its mothers breast.

10-097-P05

On Spirit wings afar
To turn each else baneful ray
That its purity might mar.

10-097-P06

That Springs within its mind
Lest all thats lovely comes to nought
Which speaks its will divine,

10-097-P07
But alas! what are Angels tears?
Or what can they avail?
When through the blight of after years
We read the hearts sad tale.
